human.summary: A warmer climate can make heat, floods and drought more damaging to daily life. People may need more protection at work and more energy to keep homes safe.
consequences: Long hot periods can increase heat illness and strain the body, especially where people cannot cool down.
Heat combined with drought can reduce crops and livestock production.
Keeping buildings cool can increase electricity use and household bills in exposed cities.

planet.summary: A warmer climate changes conditions across land, oceans and ice. Many species and habitats face several pressures at once.
consequences: Some species lose places cool enough for them to survive.
Less snow and ice changes how much sunlight is reflected and when fresh water reaches rivers.
Repeated or stronger heat can exceed the conditions that ecosystems can recover from.

economy.hiddenCost: More warming increases damage to health, food supplies, water, buildings and nature. Those costs are often missing from the price of the activities releasing heat-trapping gases.
economy.whoPays: People with little money or protection often have the hardest time recovering. This includes places that released little of the pollution causing the warming.
economy.physicalLimit: There is no single temperature at which the whole economy fails. To stop adding warming from carbon dioxide, human releases must fall to the amount removed and stored.
economy.defaultDriver: Burning coal, oil and gas, clearing land and continuing to use high-emissions equipment add heat-trapping gases to the air.
systemLevers: Cut emissions across power, transport, buildings, farming and industry.
Fund protection for exposed communities, while cutting carbon dioxide and other heat-trapping gases.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: This gas adds strongly to warming over the near term. It also helps form ground-level ozone, which can affect breathing and crops.
consequences: Added warming can make dangerous hot periods more severe within the lifetimes of today's buildings and services.
Ozone can damage plants and worsen breathing problems in exposed populations.
Food prices can become less dependable when heat and ozone reduce harvests together.

planet.summary: Rapid warming from this gas can put ecosystems under pressure before they have time to adjust. Its contribution to ground-level ozone can also damage plants.
consequences: Faster change can push some ecosystems beyond their capacity to recover.
Ozone can harm plant tissue and reduce the way crops and wild plants use sunlight.
Added warming increases pressure on ice and frozen soils, which can reinforce further change.

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: A rise in methane concentration is not the same as the amount people emitted. Natural releases and the methane removed from the air must also be accounted for.
economy.defaultDriver: Warmer, waterlogged ground can help microbes produce more methane, and thawing can expose stored plant material. Water conditions and the breakdown of the gas affect how much reaches the air. The size of this response remains uncertain.
systemLevers: Finding gas leaks can reduce methane releases when operators repair them and check that the repair worked. Measuring a leak by itself does not stop it.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Losing forests can disrupt the water, food and income that nearby communities depend on. The consequences vary with how the cleared land and remaining forest are managed.
consequences: Dry-season fires and smoke can damage homes and harm breathing.
Changes in the water trees return to the air can make local or regional rainfall less dependable.
People may lose forest products, jobs and some natural protection from floods.

planet.summary: Removing forests takes away habitat, stored carbon and the role trees play in moving water. Remaining patches may become less able to withstand further damage.
consequences: Isolated habitats leave some species with fewer places to move or breed.
Less moisture returned by trees can contribute to drying and fire exposure in affected regions.
Cleared or damaged land may take up less carbon than the forest it replaces.

economy.hiddenCost: Clearing trees can remove wildlife habitat, stored carbon and benefits such as cleaner water. Income from timber or farming does not necessarily cover those losses.
economy.whoPays: People who depend on forests, including Indigenous communities, can lose food, income and cultural places. Water users farther downstream can also be affected.
economy.physicalLimit: There is no universal amount of clearing that makes every forest collapse. Recovery depends on remaining trees, soil, fire, rainfall and connections between habitats.
economy.defaultDriver: Expanding farmland is the main direct cause globally. Roads, mining, demand for products and weak protection of land rights also contribute.
systemLevers: Track where products come from and enforce rules against clearing natural forests.
Protect community land rights and existing forests. Restore damaged land with suitable native species.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Large-scale crop and livestock production supplies food but can also concentrate pollution, health and worker risks. Farmers, workers and consumers can be affected when water, animal health or feed become unreliable.
consequences: Nutrients leaving fields can pollute rivers and make drinking water harder to treat.
Heat can make farm work unsafe and harm livestock health and production.
Rising fertiliser or feed prices and animal disease can raise food costs.

planet.summary: Large-scale crop and livestock production can put nearby water and habitats under pressure through fertilizer, manure, feed production and land use. Effects depend on farming methods and the surrounding landscape.
consequences: Nutrients washed downstream can feed algae and reduce oxygen as they decay.
Large areas of one crop can support fewer kinds of pollinating insects and wildlife.
Loss of soil organic material can make land less able to retain water and recover from stress.

economy.hiddenCost: Food prices may leave out damage from water overuse, pollution, lost habitat and heat-trapping gases. Health and working conditions also affect the wider cost of food production.
economy.whoPays: Farm workers, small producers, low-income consumers and people using water downstream may bear costs they did not choose.
economy.physicalLimit: Farms depend on usable soil, water, nutrients and tolerable heat. Limits differ by crop, production method and place.
economy.defaultDriver: Subsidies, buying rules and demand can reward producing more even when soil, water or health are harmed.
systemLevers: Reduce avoidable fertilizer losses, livestock emissions and damage to soils using locally tested methods.
Support farming that protects water, health and habitat, and reduce food waste without harming nutrition or incomes.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Demand for farm products can put pressure on land and water when supply expands faster than those resources can support. Households feel the effects through food costs and reliability.
consequences: Prices can rise when demand grows faster than available food supply.
More crop and grazing land can mean more clearing and water use.
Places relying on imported food are exposed when harvest failures disrupt their suppliers.

planet.summary: Demand for meat, animal feed and other farm products can encourage expansion onto forest land. This is less likely when existing farmland, higher yields or effective protection meet the demand without new clearing.
consequences: Producing and delivering food uses machinery, plant nutrients, refrigeration and transport. Fossil fuels and fossil-generated electricity used in these steps release carbon dioxide.

economy.hiddenCost: Producing what people eat can bring costs from land clearing, water use and pollution. Diet-related illness can add further costs, depending on the foods and people involved.
economy.whoPays: Farm workers, nearby communities, consumers and health services can share different parts of the burden.
economy.physicalLimit: Food production depends on suitable land, water and healthy soil. Expanding production by clearing natural habitat can weaken these supports. The outcome varies by place.
economy.defaultDriver: Prices, farm support and the products available in shops shape demand. They do not always reflect the full effects of producing food.
systemLevers: Support varied, nutritious foods with lower land and emissions demands where appropriate.
Protect natural habitats in food supply chains and reduce food lost between farms, shops and homes.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Growing cities need housing, water, drains, trees and transport to keep pace. When those services lag, more people can end up exposed to heat or flooding.
consequences: Paving without enough shade and drainage can leave neighbourhoods hotter and more flood-prone.
Water, sanitation and transport services can become strained.
Rapid growth can increase housing costs and pressure on residents to move.

planet.summary: City growth changes housing, transport, industry and energy use at the same time. Emissions can rise or fall depending on these choices, and some activity may shift into neighbouring regions.
consequences: Outward growth of homes, roads and other city facilities can replace forest with built land. This is one part of overall forest loss, not an explanation for all of it.
City growth can increase water demand and pollution both inside and outside city boundaries. Better services, more efficient use and changes in industry can moderate or reverse the increase.

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: Expanding an administrative boundary does not mean new land was built on. Different map versions must be made comparable before measuring change.
economy.defaultDriver: The growth of towns and cities as more people live and work in them. Replacing plants and soil with buildings and roads can trap heat and leave rainwater with fewer places to soak into the ground. Planning and public services affect how these changes are managed.
systemLevers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.
Fund practical support and monitor who can actually access it, especially where people have few alternatives.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: The low purchase price of short-lived clothing can leave costs elsewhere. Communities making, handling and disposing of it may face polluted water, unsafe work and growing waste.
consequences: Untreated factory wastewater can pollute rivers used for drinking or farming.
Low-paid workers may face harmful exposures and insecure income.
Large volumes of discarded clothing can overwhelm waste services and add to unsafe burning or dumping.

planet.summary: Making and transporting large volumes of short-lived clothing uses energy. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, it releases carbon dioxide.
consequences: Frequently replacing clothing increases demand for fibres, water, energy and processing chemicals. Resources are used to make replacements while existing clothes may still be usable.
High demand for leather and plant-based clothing fibres can add pressure to clear forests. This link depends on where materials come from and whether supply chains avoid newly cleared land.

economy.hiddenCost: Frequent replacement of cheap clothing creates waste and pollution costs beyond its shop price. Small fibres can escape during production, washing and disposal.
economy.whoPays: Communities near factories and waste sites, workers and water-treatment services can face burdens that clothing prices do not cover.
economy.physicalLimit: Keeping fibres and harmful chemicals out of water requires changes in materials, production and treatment. No single recycling or filtering step solves every textile problem.
economy.defaultDriver: Rapid product turnover and low prices encourage making and discarding more clothing.
systemLevers: Make clothing last longer and support repair, reuse and responsible collection.
Require producers to address waste and chemical releases, with treatment suited to the pollutants present.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: People forced to move may lose their homes, income and support networks. Receiving communities need enough housing and services to help newcomers settle safely.
consequences: Children's schooling and families' access to regular care can be interrupted.
Water supplies, clinics and affordable housing may face extra demand.
Competition for land, jobs or aid can add tension, though conflict is not inevitable.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.
domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established

economy.hiddenCost: Damage to housing and repeated disruption can create repair, temporary accommodation and moving costs. The burden depends on insurance, public support and safe alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Residents, landlords, insurers and public services may share the bill. People with little savings or secure housing can have fewer recovery options.
economy.physicalLimit: Not all migration is caused by climate. Do not add new movements to the number of people already displaced as if they were the same kind of count.
economy.defaultDriver: Repeated periods of heat and humidity can make work and daily life unsafe. They can contribute to pressure to move, alongside jobs, housing, family ties and other factors.
systemLevers: Moving before repeated disasters destroy homes can reduce emergency displacement. The benefit depends on providing a safe, supported destination and involving the people who move.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Shrinking local water, soil and material reserves can make essential supplies harder or more expensive to obtain. Households and farms with few alternatives are more exposed.
consequences: Falling groundwater can raise pumping costs and make wells less dependable.
Losing fertile soil can reduce harvests and increase spending on farming inputs.
Cities, farms and ecosystems may compete for the same limited resources.

planet.summary: Using water, soil and other reserves faster than they recover can weaken ecosystems that depend on them.
consequences: Falling groundwater can reduce flow to rivers and wetlands.
Damaged soil may support less life and cope less well with drought.
Already depleted systems can take longer to recover after a climate shock.

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: Material use does not measure remaining reserves, scarcity or the quality of ore. It is also different from extraction alone or recycled content. Missing areas and material groups must not be counted as zero.
economy.defaultDriver: Mining and processing draw on materials, land, water and energy. The amount needed depends on technology, recycled inputs and what activities are counted.
systemLevers: Removing carbon dioxide can require land, water, energy and materials. The demands differ greatly between methods and can create pressure on other resources.
Designing buildings to use less concrete can reduce demand for newly extracted materials. Changing the cement recipe alone does not guarantee lower material use.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Releasing this gas adds to warming that can last across decades. The consequences can reach people's health, homes, food supplies and public services.
consequences: Added warming can increase damaging heat, fire, flooding and rising-sea hazards.
Public budgets may face more spending on protection and disaster recovery.
Households with fewer resources can find cooling, insurance, repairs or relocation harder to afford.
populations: Children living through long warming horizons

planet.summary: The gas builds up in the atmosphere and adds long-lasting warming. Oceans also absorb some of it, changing seawater chemistry.
consequences: Continued releases increase the warming burden that future ecosystems face.
Warmer and more acidic water can put marine life under pressure.
Ice loss and weaker carbon uptake can reinforce parts of the wider climate response.

economy.hiddenCost: Releasing carbon dioxide adds to future warming damage. The price paid for fuel or industrial products often leaves out those costs.
economy.whoPays: Exposed households, workers, public services and future generations share the damage unevenly.
economy.physicalLimit: Warming from carbon dioxide depends strongly on the total released over time. A chosen warming limit therefore leaves a limited amount that can still be emitted.
economy.defaultDriver: Existing fossil-fuel equipment, subsidies and long investment cycles can keep emissions high even when cleaner options exist.
systemLevers: Use energy sources that release less heat-trapping gas. Use less energy to do the same job and cut waste.
Combine standards, investment and fair financial support so workers and households can make the change.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Daily life built around private vehicles can expose people to exhaust, fuel-price changes and high travel costs. Street design also affects safety and access for people who do not drive.
consequences: People near busy roads may breathe more pollution that harms the lungs and heart.
A fuel-price rise is harder to manage when every essential journey requires driving.
Roads and parking can reduce space for safe walking, cycling and shaded public places.

planet.summary: Petrol and diesel vehicles release carbon dioxide as they burn fuel. Electric vehicles shift much of the emissions from use to electricity production, while making vehicles and roads adds separate emissions.
consequences: Car-oriented development often needs large areas of roads and parking. Dark paved surfaces can store daytime heat, although shade, reflective materials and compact design can reduce this effect. Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight during the day and releases stored heat later. Large paved areas can keep nearby places warmer after sunset.

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: A journey count alone cannot tell us fuel use, emissions, delay or exposure. Each needs its own supporting activity data.
economy.defaultDriver: The vehicles people use for their own journeys, such as cars and motorcycles. Burning petrol or diesel releases gases that warm the planet and pollution that affects air quality. The impact depends on the vehicle, its energy source and how far and often it travels.
systemLevers: Frequent, affordable buses and trains can give people an alternative to private vehicles. The service must connect the places people need to reach.
Safe, connected routes make it easier to walk or cycle for short journeys. This can reduce the need to use a private vehicle.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Several hazards arriving together or in sequence can damage homes and interrupt daily life. Repeated losses can make recovery harder than a single event.
consequences: Storms, fires and floods can interrupt roads, electricity and housing.
Schooling, medical care and work may be disrupted during emergencies.
Repeated damage can make insurance harder to obtain and leave communities less able to rebuild.

planet.summary: Repeated or combined hazards can change which species survive and how habitats are structured. Recovery becomes harder when disturbances arrive too close together.
consequences: An ecosystem may not return to its earlier condition between events.
Species tolerant of heat, fire or flooding may replace less tolerant ones.
Repeated storms, fires or coral damage can reduce the variety of shelter and feeding places.

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: This counts one specific combination of heat and heavy rain, not every combined climate hazard. Do not count a day if either reading is missing or the events fall outside the chosen time window.
economy.defaultDriver: A warmer climate changes the chances and strength of several hazards, including heat and heavy rain. Some can occur together and worsen one another, with different effects in different regions.
systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Changes in tropical Pacific water can shift rain and ocean conditions far away. People may feel the effects through farming, fishing, water supplies and prices.
consequences: Drought can damage crops in some places while floods damage them elsewhere.
Changes in sea temperature and nutrients can disrupt fisheries.
Food and water supplies can become less dependable within an affected season.

planet.summary: Warm tropical Pacific conditions change the exchange of heat and water between ocean and air. Effects can reach distant marine and land ecosystems.
consequences: Less deep, nutrient-rich water reaching the surface can reduce marine plant growth.
Persistently warm water can increase coral bleaching risk.
Changes in distant rainfall can expose land ecosystems to drought or floods.

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: When updates are missing, retain the last reviewed value and show its age and source gap. Do not change the score to fill the gap.
economy.defaultDriver: Weaker east-to-west winds over the equatorial Pacific allow warm surface water to move east. This can reinforce warming in the central and eastern Pacific.
systemLevers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Cooler tropical Pacific conditions can shift rainfall so some regions face drought while others receive damaging rain. Impacts differ between places and events.
consequences: Changes in seasonal rain can make water supplies harder to plan around.
Flood losses may increase in some river basins while drought losses rise elsewhere.
Farming and electricity from dams can both be affected during the same climate cycle.

planet.summary: Cool tropical Pacific conditions shift seasonal rain and ocean patterns. Different regions can face drying or flooding during the same event.
consequences: Water extremes can strain ecosystems adapted to more usual conditions.
Changes in rain timing can disrupt seasonal growth and breeding.
Fire danger may rise in some regions while flooding increases elsewhere.

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: When updates are missing, retain the last reviewed value and show its age and source gap. Do not change the score to fill the gap.
economy.defaultDriver: Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions.
systemLevers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Changes in the large Atlantic circulation can shift regional rainfall, coastal water levels and marine conditions. This creates uncertainty for communities planning food, water and coastal protection.
consequences: Rainfall changes can affect farms and water supplies around the North Atlantic and in the tropics.
Changes in marine food webs may affect fishing livelihoods.
Energy and coastal planning become harder when regional conditions change in unexpected ways.

planet.summary: Changes in Atlantic circulation move heat and nutrients differently. Marine habitats and rainfall patterns can change over wide areas.
consequences: Species may face different temperatures, food supplies and currents.
The regional distribution of rain can shift as ocean heat transport changes.
Some changes could be abrupt, but their timing and scale remain uncertain.

economy.hiddenCost: Changes in Atlantic heat transport can alter regional rainfall and coastal water levels. Farms and infrastructure may need costly changes as a result.
economy.whoPays: Farmers, coastal communities and public services may face adjustment costs that depend on regional changes.
economy.physicalLimit: The cited evidence does not establish a universal collapse threshold at 1.5°C. The size and timing of future weakening remain uncertain.
economy.defaultDriver: Warming and added freshwater affect the sinking of seawater in the North Atlantic. Planning based only on past conditions can leave communities exposed.
systemLevers: Include a range of possible circulation changes in coastal and water planning.
Improve ocean observations and prepare farming and food supplies for less predictable conditions.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Hot, humid air makes sweat less effective at cooling the body. Dangerous exposure can develop more quickly when people are active or have no access to cooler conditions.
consequences: Severe exposure can cause heat illness and put organs under strain.
Farm, construction and delivery workers may have fewer hours when work is safe.
An electricity failure can become especially dangerous if it removes the only effective cooling.

planet.summary: This measure describes conditions that make it harder for people to lose heat. It does not by itself measure damage to ecosystems. Effects on other living things need separate evidence.
domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established

economy.hiddenCost: Hot, humid conditions can reduce safe working time and increase illness and healthcare costs. These losses may extend beyond recorded deaths during heatwaves.
economy.whoPays: Outdoor workers and people without safe cooling are especially exposed. Families and health services also carry costs.
economy.physicalLimit: There is no single safe temperature for everyone. Humidity, work, age, health, clothing and access to cooling all affect how well the body loses heat.
economy.defaultDriver: Warming raises heat exposure, while unequal shade, housing, cooling and worker protection shape who is harmed.
systemLevers: Provide enforceable work-rest arrangements, shade and access to safe cooling.
Improve efficient cooling in exposed homes and use building and street design to reduce heat.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Unreliable seasonal rains make it harder to time planting, manage reservoirs and prepare for floods. Farmers and households can face losses and changing food prices.
consequences: Rain arriving too early, too late or in uneven bursts can damage harvests.
Flooding and dry breaks can affect the same river basin within one season.
Water storage and electricity from dams become harder to manage when rainfall timing changes.

planet.summary: Many ecosystems depend on seasonal rains arriving at a reasonably predictable time. Changes in timing and intensity can disrupt growth and recovery.
consequences: Plants and animals may lose the usual rhythm of wet and dry seasons.
Alternating floods and dry breaks can erode soils and damage freshwater habitats.
Wetlands and rivers may become less dependable places for seasonal growth.

economy.hiddenCost: Rain arriving too late, in damaging bursts or with long breaks can reduce harvests and income. Families may need to borrow more or buy food they normally grow.
economy.whoPays: Rain-dependent farmers and households with limited savings can be hit hard. Governments may face extra food and disaster-response costs.
economy.physicalLimit: Crops need water at particular stages. Later rain cannot always undo damage from an earlier dry spell, but outcomes depend on the crop and season.
economy.defaultDriver: Warming and changes over land and ocean affect seasonal rain. Farming and reservoirs can remain planned around older rainfall patterns.
systemLevers: Provide useful local forecasts and access to seeds suited to variable rain.
Improve water planning and fair emergency credit so a failed season does not create lasting debt.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Ground that thaws and shifts can damage Arctic homes and essential services. Remote communities may have few alternatives when roads or water systems fail.
consequences: Buildings, roads and storage tanks can lose support as ice in the ground melts.
Damaged drinking-water or sewage systems can increase contamination risks.
Travel routes and access to hunting, fishing or other local supplies may become less dependable.

planet.summary: Thawing northern soils changes both the shape of the land and the fate of stored carbon. These changes can affect habitats and add to warming.
consequences: Previously frozen plant material becomes more available for decay and gas release.
Melting ground ice can form hollows and ponds that change drainage and habitat.
Carbon stored for long periods may no longer remain safely frozen.

economy.hiddenCost: Thawing ground can damage buildings and release carbon that adds to warming. Both create costs beyond those of repairing a single site.
economy.whoPays: Northern residents, infrastructure owners and public services face repair costs. Added warming has wider consequences.
economy.physicalLimit: Ice-rich ground may sink as its ice melts. The amount of sinking and carbon released depends on local soil, water and temperature. It is not a fixed share everywhere.
economy.defaultDriver: Rapid northern warming changes ground conditions faster than some buildings and roads were designed to handle.
systemLevers: Include emissions from thawing ground in climate planning and improve local monitoring.
Use foundations and land-use rules suited to the ground, and avoid building on unstable ice-rich sites.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Rain adds weight and liquid water to existing snow and can weaken its layers. On steep slopes, this may trigger a slide of wet snow. Avalanches can bury or damage roads, railways, power lines and communications equipment. Repeated closures are especially disruptive where few alternative mountain routes exist.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Rain adds weight and liquid water to existing snow and can weaken its layers. On steep slopes, this may trigger a slide of wet snow.
domains: ice, snow, frozen ground, and albedo

economy.hiddenCost: Service interruptions can bring repair costs, lost working time and spending on backup supplies. Wider losses depend on how long the interruption lasts and which activities rely on it.
economy.whoPays: Service operators, customers, workers and public budgets can share the costs. People without alternative services are more exposed to disruption.
economy.physicalLimit: Rain falling on snow does not prove that a flood occurred.
economy.defaultDriver: Warming can turn some winter snowfall into rain and increase melting. Where rain falls on stored snow, the combined water can raise flood risk, depending on the snow, soil and drainage.
systemLevers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: After a glacier basin passes its period of greatest meltwater supply, the contribution can decline over time. People and power systems relying on that water may face less dependable dry-season flows.
consequences: Strong seasonal meltwater flows carry fine rock particles from glaciers. The amount and timing of sediment depend on the flow, rather than simply on whether a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff. Sediment carried into a reservoir settles as the water slows. Continued build-up takes up storage space and can interfere with water intakes.

planet.summary: Meltwater carries fine rock and soil into the water below glaciers. How much arrives, and at what depth, depends on the amount of water and how it enters the basin.
consequences: Strong seasonal meltwater flows carry fine rock particles from glaciers. The amount and timing of sediment depend on the flow, rather than simply on whether a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.
domains: ice, snow, frozen ground, and albedo

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: Keep the last reviewed basin finding and show when its evidence is old. Global temperature alone cannot show that a basin has passed this point.
economy.defaultDriver: At first, faster melting can send more glacier water into rivers. Continued ice loss eventually leaves less ice to melt, so the long-term water contribution declines in affected river basins.
systemLevers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Some marine germs can cause illness through seafood or contact with open wounds. Their spread can add pressure to coastal health services. This is an infection pathway, rather than heat injury itself.

planet.summary: Changing water conditions can alter where disease-causing organisms survive and spread. Effects differ by organism and host, and a wider detected range does not prove disease increased everywhere.
domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: Do not claim a change in geographic range without both environmental coverage and a traceable disease-reporting source.
economy.defaultDriver: Prolonged warm seawater can help some disease-causing germs grow in new places or seasons. Salt content, human or animal contact and other local conditions also matter.
systemLevers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: When warm surface water mixes less with deeper coastal water, oxygen and habitat conditions can worsen. Fishing communities may face less dependable catches and seafood supplies.
consequences: Weak mixing can make low-oxygen conditions and some algae problems more likely.
Young fish and shellfish may lose suitable habitat as oxygen-rich areas shrink.
Closures and changes in catch or seafood quality can affect local incomes.

planet.summary: Strongly separated water layers mix less easily, slowing the oxygen supply to the bottom. Oxygen can run low as organisms continue to use it, especially where much organic material is decaying.
consequences: Separated layers in warm river-mouth waters can make oxygen shortages worse. Young fish and shellfish may then have less suitable sheltered habitat.
More strongly separated water layers slow the replacement of oxygen below the surface. Low-oxygen conditions are more likely where excess organic material is also using up oxygen as it decays.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life

economy.hiddenCost: Poorer mixing between upper and deeper seawater can reduce suitable habitat before a major loss of fish is visible. Fishing income may become less dependable.
economy.whoPays: Coastal fishers, shellfish growers and communities relying on seafood can be affected first.
economy.physicalLimit: Deeper water needs enough mixing or circulation to replace oxygen used by living things. The amount needed differs across waters and species.
economy.defaultDriver: Warmer surface water can strengthen the separation between layers. Fisheries planning may not keep up with the changing habitat.
systemLevers: Monitor water temperature, oxygen and mixing together.
Reduce excess nutrients entering vulnerable waters and adjust fishing rules to observed habitat conditions.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Salt moving farther up a river mouth can affect water supplies before land is permanently flooded. Households, farms and utilities may need costlier ways to obtain fresh water.
consequences: Utilities may need to blend water or switch intakes when salt levels rise.
Farmers can lose a reliable source of fresh irrigation water.
Shallow wells may become salty and less useful even while they still contain water.

planet.summary: Saltier water reaching drinking-water intakes can exceed normal treatment capabilities. Utilities may need to change intake locations, blend supplies or use additional treatment.
consequences: Saltwater moving inland can enter shallow freshwater stores near the coast. The layer of usable fresh water may then become thinner.
Salt moving through river mouths can also reach connected underground water. This can make coastal wells and reserves saltier.

economy.hiddenCost: Salt moving inland can make drinking water and irrigation more expensive even when water is still physically present.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers and utilities near river mouths may need treatment, storage or another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: When river flow is too weak to hold seawater back, salt can move past water intakes or into connected groundwater. Local geography matters.
economy.defaultDriver: Rising seas, low river flow and withdrawals can increase the problem, especially where planning treats it as only a short storm event.
systemLevers: Track salt levels and adjust water intakes and releases before supplies become unusable.
Protect needed freshwater flows and redesign repeatedly exposed intakes where practical.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: When deep, nutrient-rich water stops reaching the surface at the usual time, coastal food supplies can change. Fishing communities may face less predictable catches and income.
consequences: Less nutrient supply can reduce the growth of tiny plants at the base of the food web.
Fish catches may arrive at different times or in different amounts.
Communities relying on a short fishing season can have few alternatives when it fails.
populations: Port towns tied to seasonal catch

planet.summary: When less deep water reaches the surface, fewer nutrients may be available to tiny sunlit-water organisms. Their growth can decline, reducing food at the base of marine food chains.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life

economy.hiddenCost: Changes in the arrival of nutrients at the sea surface can make catches and fishing income less reliable.
economy.whoPays: Fishing families, seafood processors and coastal consumers are affected where local food supplies depend on these productive waters.
economy.physicalLimit: Nutrients must reach sunlit water at useful times to support the food web. Fish catches also depend on fishing pressure and other conditions.
economy.defaultDriver: Winds and ocean conditions can shift while fishing seasons and markets remain based on past patterns.
systemLevers: Connect ocean monitoring with flexible fishing decisions.
Prepare ports and coastal businesses for changing catch seasons and support other income options where needed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Very heavy rain can overwhelm airport drains and reduce visibility. Flights and ground operations may be delayed or cancelled.
consequences: Intense rain can arrive faster than the ground can absorb it or drains and rivers can carry it away. Water can then rise quickly and flood nearby areas. Rapid floods can wash dirt and pollution into water sources or damage intakes. Treatment plants may need extra cleaning steps or temporary interruptions.

A heavy burst of rain can send more water into pipes and treatment plants than they can handle. The excess may back up or spill out. Overflowing sewage systems can expose people to water carrying harmful germs. Outbreak risk rises when treatment and sanitation no longer contain that exposure.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Intense rain can arrive faster than the ground can absorb it or drains and rivers can carry it away. Water can then rise quickly and flood nearby areas.
consequences: A heavy burst of rain can send more water into pipes and treatment plants than they can handle. The excess may back up or spill out.
Heavy rain and runoff can make local surface seawater fresher and lighter. This can briefly reduce mixing with deeper water when winds and currents are weak.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: A daily grid value is not a measurement of a short local downpour. Withhold locations with less than 95% of days complete, keep the last validated complete year and show its age. Missing days are not rain-free days.
economy.defaultDriver: Warmer air can hold more water vapour. When suitable storms form, that extra moisture can fall as heavier rain or snow. Warming does not make every place wetter.
systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

human.summary: A rapidly strengthening cyclone gives ships and ports less time to prepare. Closures, changed routes and delays may increase.
consequences: A storm that strengthens quickly near land can leave less preparation time. Strong winds, heavy rain and high seawater levels may then combine to produce flooding. Coastal flooding can affect cable landing stations and their power or land connections. Shared locations increase the risk of several links failing together, while protection, backup power and separated routes can prevent disruption.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: A storm that strengthens quickly near land can leave less preparation time. Strong winds, heavy rain and high seawater levels may then combine to produce flooding.
consequences: Powerful cyclone waves and currents can break or overturn corals and move reef rubble. Damage depends on the storm's path and the reef exposed to it.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life

economy.hiddenCost: Service interruptions can bring repair costs, lost working time and spending on backup supplies. Wider losses depend on how long the interruption lasts and which activities rely on it.
economy.whoPays: Service operators, customers, workers and public budgets can share the costs. People without alternative services are more exposed to disruption.
economy.physicalLimit: If new readings are unavailable, keep the last reviewed value and show its age and missing coverage. Do not change the score to fill the gap.
economy.defaultDriver: Warmer ocean and air conditions can provide more energy and moisture to an organized tropical storm. This can favour rapid strengthening, but it does not determine what any individual storm will do.
systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

human.summary: Some observed high-altitude smoke events temporarily cooled Earth's surface overall. The result depends on particle type, height, lifetime, clouds and the surface below, so the effect is not always cooling. Hotter air can make aircraft takeoff more difficult and put extra strain on runways and ground operations. The effects depend on the aircraft, airport and conditions.
consequences: Some powerful fire clouds carry smoke high into the atmosphere, where particles can remain longer. This adds to the particle layer rather than removing its cooling influence, although different smoke components can have different effects. Some airborne particles have partly offset warming by reflecting sunlight. Removing that cooling influence can add near-term warming unless the warming influence of other gases also falls enough.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Some powerful fire clouds carry smoke high into the atmosphere, where particles can remain longer. This adds to the particle layer rather than removing its cooling influence, although different smoke components can have different effects.
consequences: Some observed high-altitude smoke events temporarily cooled Earth's surface overall. The result depends on particle type, height, lifetime, clouds and the surface below, so the effect is not always cooling.

economy.physicalLimit: Do not combine different pollutants or substitute emissions for the concentration people or ecosystems encounter. Missing observations do not mean clean conditions.

systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

human.summary: Rapid erosion and collapsing coastal slopes can remove support beneath buildings, roads and pipes. Communities may lose reliable access and essential services. Damage to roads, power lines or utilities in remote polar areas can interrupt essential services. Difficult access and limited alternatives can make recovery harder.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Rapid erosion and collapsing coastal slopes can remove support beneath buildings, roads and pipes. Communities may lose reliable access and essential services.
domains: ice, snow, frozen ground, and albedo

economy.hiddenCost: Service interruptions can bring repair costs, lost working time and spending on backup supplies. Wider losses depend on how long the interruption lasts and which activities rely on it.
economy.whoPays: Service operators, customers, workers and public budgets can share the costs. People without alternative services are more exposed to disruption.
economy.physicalLimit: Temperature alone does not show how far a coastline has retreated.
economy.defaultDriver: Melting ice inside frozen coastal ground weakens the land. Waves can then wear it away more easily, especially where less sea ice leaves the shore exposed.
systemLevers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

human.summary: Limited water can bring animals together around fewer drinking places and make cleaning harder. Poorer water quality and closer contact can increase the spread of disease.
consequences: When reliable water supply cannot meet normal demand, utilities may ask or require people to use less. The restrictions depend on local operating decisions.

planet.summary: When water use is already close to available supply, seasonal or drought-related changes can leave lakes and reservoirs short. Imports, lower demand and careful operation can sometimes keep storage stable.

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: Missing withdrawal records are not zero use. A whole-basin ratio does not describe one household or facility.
economy.defaultDriver: Irrigated farms draw water from supplies also needed by households, businesses and rivers. Heavy use can leave less available during dry periods.
systemLevers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.
consequences: Falling groundwater supplies can force use of poorer-quality water or change how salty water moves. Soil salt levels can rise where irrigation and drainage allow salts to collect. Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living

planet.summary: Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.

economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: A missing well or reading does not show that groundwater is stable.
economy.defaultDriver: Pumping water for crops can reduce underground reserves when use exceeds the water that seeps back in. The shortage can build up over years, making wells less reliable.
systemLevers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

human.summary: A surge in heat illness and deaths may occur alongside overwhelming demand for ambulances and hospitals. Death counts alone do not show whether services were overloaded. Their workload and capacity need separate evidence.

planet.summary: The documented effects here concern people, livelihoods or essential services. A separate direct effect on climate or natural ecosystems has not been established by this evidence.

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: Keep the last validated release and show when it is old. Temperature exposure alone cannot establish heat-related deaths. Missing uncertainty intervals are not zero uncertainty, and different definitions of mortality must not be combined.
economy.defaultDriver: Power disconnection can remove cooling or interrupt essential home medical equipment during extreme heat. This can increase the risk of death, especially for people with limited alternatives or existing illness.
systemLevers: Heat warnings can help prevent deaths when they trigger contact with vulnerable people, access to cooling and health-service preparation. An alert alone is not enough.
City plans can help prevent heat-related deaths when forecasts trigger funded action. This includes reaching vulnerable people, opening cooling spaces and protecting outdoor workers.
Making safe indoor temperatures available to people at greatest risk can help prevent heat-related deaths. Cooling must remain affordable and available when needed.
Insulation, shade and ventilation can reduce dangerous indoor heat when upgrades suit the local climate and allow heat to escape. Lower exposure can reduce estimated heat-related death risks.

human.summary: Breathing polluted air can increase heart and lung illness and shorten lives. Families may face treatment costs and time away from work or school.

planet.summary: The main measure here concerns harm to people from polluted air. Effects on plants, water and climate depend on the pollutants and require separate measurements.
domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established

economy.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
economy.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.
economy.physicalLimit: Keep the last validated World Health Organization release and show its age. Pollution concentration alone cannot establish the number of deaths caused, and missing estimates must not become zero.
economy.defaultDriver: Traffic releases particles and gases that people breathe. Exposure to this pollution can contribute to lung and heart disease, depending on the level and duration.
systemLevers: Connect useful warnings with accessible health services and practical protection for exposed people.
Improve access to safe housing, water or cooling where the documented exposure requires it.

human.summary: People working in hot conditions may need more rest and may be unable to work safely for as long. Risks depend on the task, humidity, clothing and available protection.

systemLevers: City heat plans can protect workers when they include enforceable rules and practical support for safer work. A plan without workplace measures may leave this exposure unchanged.

human.summary: Large computing facilities need dependable electricity and cooling. Rapid growth can put pressure on local power, water and land systems.
consequences: New electricity demand may require expensive network upgrades.
Water used for cooling can compete with household, farming or environmental needs.
Backup generators and construction traffic can add local noise and air pollution.

planet.summary: Computing facilities have a physical footprint through electricity, cooling water and construction. Impacts depend strongly on energy sources and local water conditions.
consequences: Continuous demand can prolong fossil generation where cleaner supply is insufficient.
Cooling can add pressure to water already shared with ecosystems.
Concentrated construction uses land and supporting equipment.

Water-intensive cooling can add competition in already dry river basins.
Limited local power capacity can make reliability harder to maintain during hot weather.

consequences: Fossil-fuel generation may continue where new cleaner power cannot keep pace.
Water-intensive cooling can add to stress on rivers and other water users.
More hardware creates demand for materials and chip manufacturing.

Air emissions, wastewater and workplace chemicals need effective controls.
Companies depending on the same factories can experience supply problems together.

consequences: Factories can place large water and energy demands in the same industrial region.
Heat-trapping process gases and local pollutants need separate controls.
Concentrated production makes the effects of a few facilities significant for the wider supply chain.

consequences: Broken routes or switching systems can interrupt communication across a wide area.
Operating and expanding networks uses electricity.
A lost connection can disrupt shops, deliveries and the way emergency teams work together.

consequences: Moving and switching data uses energy across a distributed network.
Growing traffic requires equipment and supporting facilities.
A network failure is not by itself evidence of damage to a natural ecosystem.

Households still need a working local connection even when major internet routes are available.
Adding more equipment uses materials and ongoing electricity.

consequences: More sites require more equipment and maintenance.
Backup fuel use can add emissions where normal power is unreliable.

Independent backup routes matter more than simply counting the number of sites.

Services described as being in the cloud still depend on vulnerable physical equipment.

Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Aircraft release carbon dioxide when they burn jet fuel. The total applies to the flights and fuel use included in the source's accounting. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

planet.summary: Aircraft and cargo can move living organisms to places they would not normally reach. Most do not establish harmful populations, so flight numbers cannot be treated as a count of invasions.
consequences: Aircraft release carbon dioxide when they burn jet fuel. The total applies to the flights and fuel use included in the source's accounting.

economy.hiddenCost: Hotter air can reduce an aircraft's takeoff performance. Flights may need lighter loads, different schedules or airport changes.
economy.whoPays: Airlines, airports, passengers and freight customers can face delays and extra costs.
economy.physicalLimit: Safe loads depend on the aircraft, air temperature, airport height and runway length. Extra runway space is not always available.
economy.defaultDriver: Growing travel demand and dependence on fossil jet fuel sustain emissions, while warming adds operating challenges.
systemLevers: Use local forecasts and aircraft performance limits when planning departures.
Reduce avoidable fuel use and plan airport adaptations around local heat, flood and land constraints.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Delays and detours at sea can make ships arrive together or disrupt planned schedules. Ports may then struggle to unload, store and move the accumulated cargo.
consequences: Ship engines can produce carbon monoxide when fuel burns incompletely. A useful estimate needs details about the engine, fuel and how the vessel operates. Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.

Ships release carbon dioxide when they burn marine fuel. The total depends on vessel activity and whether the source covers domestic shipping, international shipping or both. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

planet.summary: Ship engines can release soot when they burn fuel. Winds may carry some of it to snow and ice, especially in nearby regions.
consequences: Sulfur in ship fuel can form sulfur dioxide during burning. Fuel standards and exhaust-cleaning equipment determine how much escapes.
Ship engines can produce carbon monoxide when fuel burns incompletely. A useful estimate needs details about the engine, fuel and how the vessel operates.

economy.hiddenCost: Ships burning fossil fuels release warming gases and soot. Soot settling on snow or ice can make it absorb more sunlight.
economy.whoPays: Shipping operators face the costs of cleaner equipment and fuels, while exposed communities bear pollution and climate damage.
economy.physicalLimit: The effect of soot depends on where and how much is deposited and the snow or ice conditions. There is no single reflectivity threshold for all polar waters.
economy.defaultDriver: Long-lived ships, trade demand and limited clean-fuel supply keep much shipping dependent on fossil energy.
systemLevers: Use cleaner fuels and equipment that reduce soot and heat-trapping emissions.
Plan routes and speeds to reduce fuel use and protect sensitive polar habitats.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Conventional cement production releases carbon dioxide both from heating raw materials and from the chemical change in limestone. Both sources matter within the production total. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
consequences: Making the binding ingredient in concrete releases carbon dioxide when limestone is chemically changed. This process release is separate from the fuel burned to heat the kiln. Chemically changing limestone to make cement releases carbon dioxide. Fuel used to heat the process adds a separate contribution. Both are included when assessing total production emissions.

planet.summary: Conventional cement production releases carbon dioxide both from heating raw materials and from the chemical change in limestone. Both sources matter within the production total.
consequences: Making the binding ingredient in concrete releases carbon dioxide when limestone is chemically changed. This process release is separate from the fuel burned to heat the kiln. Chemically changing limestone to make cement releases carbon dioxide. Fuel used to heat the process adds a separate contribution. Both are included when assessing total production emissions.

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: A national average does not show how one factory performs. Total production, total environmental impact and impact per unit are different measures and must remain separate.
economy.defaultDriver: More buildings and infrastructure can increase demand for cement and concrete. Reuse, material-saving design and construction standards can reduce the amount of new material needed.
systemLevers: Plan electricity supply, networks and demand together so cleaner options remain dependable.
Improve efficiency and maintain equipment, with backup arrangements suited to essential services and local hazards.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: This material supports buildings and transport, but making it can expose workers and nearby communities to heat and pollution. Replacing long-lived plants also affects industrial jobs and costs.
consequences: Each production stage needs protection suited to its machinery, heat and chemical exposures.
Polluting gases and metals from large mills require controls at their sources.
Workers and regions need time and support to adjust as older plants are replaced.

planet.summary: Conventional production uses coal, high heat and large amounts of mined material. Cleaner processes and recycling can reduce some of this footprint.
consequences: Reported greenhouse-gas totals depend on which production and energy stages are included.
Long-lived furnaces can keep coal-based methods in use for decades.
Recycled steel uses less energy in suitable electric furnaces, but scrap quality and supply limit how much new production it replaces.

economy.hiddenCost: Steel prices may leave out air pollution, climate damage and the future cost of replacing coal-based plants.
economy.whoPays: Workers and nearby communities face pollution and job changes. Consumers and public budgets may share upgrade costs.
economy.physicalLimit: Options depend on scrap quality, suitable ore, cleaner electricity or hydrogen and investment timing. No single production limit applies to every method.
economy.defaultDriver: Expensive, long-lived coal-based plants and weak demand for cleaner steel can delay change.
systemLevers: Use materials efficiently, recover good-quality scrap and expand cleaner production where supplies support it.
Plan clean energy, new equipment and support for workers together, backed by credible product standards.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Making plastics and related chemicals uses fossil raw materials and energy. Production and some disposal methods can release carbon dioxide. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
consequences: Making new plastics uses fossil raw materials, energy, water and other resources. Reuse and recycled inputs can reduce some of the demand for new material. Shortages of important resources can worsen existing tensions. Conflict risk depends strongly on how resources are shared and whether institutions can resolve disputes fairly.

Plastic entering the sea can expose animals to particles and associated chemicals. Effects on feeding relationships depend on particle type, dose and other environmental stresses. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.
domains: housing, support after moving and public services
food supplies and ways of earning a living

planet.summary: Making plastics and related chemicals uses fossil raw materials and energy. Production and some disposal methods can release carbon dioxide.
consequences: Making and handling petrochemical products can release gases from processing, storage and evaporation. The type and amount depend on the product and pollution controls.

Wear, processing and weathering can release tiny plastic fibres or fragments that enter the air. Plastic use alone does not measure airborne releases, and suspected particles need chemical confirmation.

economy.hiddenCost: Making and disposing of plastic can create pollution and emissions that are missing from its price. Some recycling methods also need substantial energy.
economy.whoPays: Nearby communities, waste workers, consumers and public waste services can share the costs.
economy.physicalLimit: Results differ by material and process. Recycling still needs energy and cannot recover every mixed or contaminated plastic product.
economy.defaultDriver: Large existing fossil-fuel factories and demand for cheap new plastic make alternatives harder to expand.
systemLevers: Reduce unnecessary material use and make products easier to reuse, collect and recycle.
Use cleaner energy and compare the full emissions of proposed production and recycling methods.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Working cooling systems can help prevent hot conditions from becoming a health emergency. Their protection depends on access, affordability and reliable power.

planet.summary: Older cooling equipment can leak CFCs or HCFCs that damage the ozone layer. This pathway excludes modern replacement gases that contain no ozone-damaging chlorine or bromine, and equipment counts alone do not measure leaks.

economy.hiddenCost: Leaks from some cooling systems release gases that strongly warm the climate. Repairs, replacement equipment and safe disposal add costs.
economy.whoPays: Households, businesses and equipment owners pay for upgrades. Climate impacts extend beyond the people using the cooling.
economy.physicalLimit: Safer alternatives must match the equipment and local conditions. Flammability, pressure, energy use and technician skills all matter.
economy.defaultDriver: Growing cooling demand and continued use of high-warming gases increase the potential for leaks.
systemLevers: Replace high-warming gases with suitable lower-impact options and improve energy efficiency.
Train technicians, check leaks and recover gases when equipment is retired.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Manufactured plant nutrients can support higher crop yields where soil nutrients limit growth. This makes repeated high-output cropping possible, alongside its other resource needs. Irrigated farms draw water from supplies also needed by households, businesses and rivers. Heavy use can leave less available during dry periods.

planet.summary: Making and using fertilisers increases the amount of nitrogen and phosphorus available in the environment. Some can escape into rivers and coastal waters if losses are not controlled.
consequences: Making nitric acid for some fertilisers produces nitrous oxide as a by-product. This link applies to that manufacturing process, not to every type of fertiliser production.

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: Keep the last validated release and show when it is old. Missing product, country or year records are not zero. Tonnes of fertiliser product must not be labelled tonnes of nutrient.
economy.defaultDriver: Growing more crops increases demand for nutrients to replace those removed at harvest. This can increase the production of manufactured fertilisers.
systemLevers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Extracting minerals directly creates demands for land, water, energy and waste management. Greater activity can increase these pressures in the places where extraction occurs. Making more batteries requires reliable supplies of mined and processed materials. Constraints and environmental pressures at those stages carry through to battery production.
consequences: Mines can directly remove forest, while their roads and settlements open nearby areas to further clearing. The wider loss depends on local development and forest protection. Clearing forests changes shade, standing water, wildlife and contact between people and insects. In some tropical settings, these changes favour mosquitoes that carry disease, but the effect is not universal.

More mining, especially of poorer-quality deposits, can require more rock, water and energy for each useful amount of mineral. Recycling and production methods affect the resulting demand for new resources. Shortages of important resources can worsen existing tensions. Conflict risk depends strongly on how resources are shared and whether institutions can resolve disputes fairly.
domains: housing, support after moving and public services

planet.summary: Mines can directly remove forest, while their roads and settlements open nearby areas to further clearing. The wider loss depends on local development and forest protection.
consequences: Collecting material from the seabed and releasing processing water can stir up fine particles. These form cloudy plumes near the bottom or within the water above it.
Mining and processing can release metals from waste, drainage and disturbed material. Some can enter water, food and animal tissues.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life
