economy.hiddenCost: Mineral extraction can affect water, land and nearby communities. The size of those impacts differs greatly between mines and extraction methods.
economy.whoPays: Local and Indigenous communities, workers and water users can bear costs, while manufacturers face supply interruptions.
economy.physicalLimit: Ore quality, water availability, waste handling and site conditions constrain production. A new extraction technology does not automatically remove every environmental cost.
economy.defaultDriver: Rising demand and limited recovery of used materials increase pressure to open or expand mines.
systemLevers: Check how each mine will use water and deal with waste. Give local people a real say in those plans.
Improve recovery, reuse and recycling, and test new extraction methods against actual local impacts.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Homes spread far from jobs and services can increase travel time, fuel costs and the cost of providing roads and utilities. Effects depend on transport choices and how neighbourhoods are planned.

planet.summary: Outward housing growth can replace vegetation with roofs, roads and other surfaces that store heat. This can increase local warming within built-up areas.
consequences: Outward housing growth often adds roads and other paved areas. Dark pavement absorbs sunlight and stores heat that is later released into the surroundings. Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight during the day and releases stored heat later. Large paved areas can keep nearby places warmer after sunset.

Building outward can remove trees and cover soil with roads and buildings. Tree cover can shrink if development does not protect existing trees or provide suitable space for replacements. Losing trees removes shade and some natural cooling. Neighbourhoods can store more daytime heat and remain warmer at night, leaving less relief for residents.

economy.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
economy.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.
economy.physicalLimit: Exposure to a hazard does not prove a service failed. Different services cannot be combined into one score without explaining how they are weighted.
economy.defaultDriver: Growing cities may spread outward into more land when housing, roads and planning favour low-density development. City growth does not always take this form.
systemLevers: Good public transport can support homes and services closer together. Housing and planning policies need to support that pattern for outward spread to slow.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Replacing fuel-burning power with lower-emissions electricity can improve air quality and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Benefits depend on which generation is actually replaced.
consequences: Nearby communities can breathe less pollution when fossil-fuel plants reduce output or close.
Less fuel use can reduce exposure to sudden fossil-fuel price rises.
Cleaner power can support lower-emissions heating, travel and industry.

planet.summary: Low-emissions electricity can reduce the climate impact of power and the activities that switch to using it. The benefit depends on replacing higher-emissions supply.
consequences: Fewer long-lived greenhouse gases are released when fossil generation is displaced.
Less fossil fuel may need to be extracted and burned.
Cleaner power enables lower-emissions heating, transport and industry.

economy.hiddenCost: Cleaner generation still needs investment in power lines, storage and suitable sites. Land and mineral impacts need careful management.
economy.whoPays: Bills, public funding and private investment determine who pays and who benefits.
economy.physicalLimit: Projects depend on equipment, skilled workers, land and dependable connections to the grid.
economy.defaultDriver: Projects depend on equipment, skilled workers, land and dependable connections to the grid.
systemLevers: Build generation and networks together, with enough dependable supply to replace high-emitting plants.
Protect communities and habitats when choosing sites and sharing benefits.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Closing coal-fired plants can reduce harmful pollution around them. Planning replacement power and support for workers helps communities share the benefits.
consequences: Less coal burning reduces fine particles and sulfur pollution.
Lower exposure can reduce related health burdens.
A planned timetable gives workers and affected regions time to prepare.

planet.summary: Retiring coal power can reduce carbon dioxide and other environmental damage when replacement generation is cleaner.
consequences: The closed plant stops its fuel-burning emissions.
Lower coal demand can reduce mining and ash-disposal pressures.
Planned replacement capacity can supply power with lower emissions.

economy.hiddenCost: Closing a plant without preparation can remove jobs, local tax income and needed electricity supply.
economy.whoPays: Workers, surrounding communities and electricity customers need a fair plan for costs and support.
economy.physicalLimit: Replacement capacity must provide dependable power when the coal plant closes.
economy.defaultDriver: Replacement capacity must provide dependable power when the coal plant closes.
systemLevers: Set closure dates alongside reliable replacement supply.
Fund retraining, pensions and new local opportunities rather than leaving communities to manage alone.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Wind, solar and other renewable sources can reduce pollution when they replace fuel-burning generation. They also give regions more ways to supply their own energy.
consequences: Avoided fuel burning can improve local air quality.
Wind and sunlight have no fuel price, which can make some operating costs steadier.
Local renewable resources can reduce dependence on imported fuels.

planet.summary: Renewable generation can reduce fossil-fuel use and emissions when it replaces existing supply. Siting and the type of technology still matter.
consequences: Power-sector greenhouse-gas releases can fall.
Less continued fossil-fuel extraction may be needed.
Some technologies use less water than fuel-burning power stations.

economy.hiddenCost: New projects need land, materials and power lines. Poor siting can harm wildlife or create conflict with nearby communities.
economy.whoPays: Investors, electricity customers and public budgets pay, while local benefit-sharing shapes fairness.
economy.physicalLimit: Useful output depends on the resource, location, network and ability to handle variable generation.
economy.defaultDriver: Useful output depends on the resource, location, network and ability to handle variable generation.
systemLevers: Coordinate new generation with transmission, storage and demand flexibility.
Choose sites with habitat protection and community participation, while improving approval processes.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Stored electricity can help bridge gaps between generation and demand. Its protection lasts only within the store's power and energy limits.
consequences: It can make supply more reliable during short gaps.
It may replace some expensive, polluting generation used at busy times.
Appropriately designed systems can keep essential services running through some outages.

planet.summary: Storage can help use low-emissions electricity that would otherwise go unused. Its own materials and energy losses still need to be considered.
consequences: Wind and solar output can be saved for later use.
Dependable stored power can replace some fossil generation.
Flexible supply supports more electric heating and transport.

economy.hiddenCost: Storage equipment has material, safety, maintenance and recycling costs. These differ across technologies.
economy.whoPays: Operators, electricity users and public funding may share costs. Market rules determine how benefits reach customers.
economy.physicalLimit: Every system has limits on how much power it supplies and for how long. Energy must first be available to store.
economy.defaultDriver: Every system has limits on how much power it supplies and for how long. Energy must first be available to store.
systemLevers: Use a mix of storage suited to the hours or days of flexibility needed.
Require safe operation, responsible mineral sourcing and recovery of materials at the end of use.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Shifting flexible electricity use can help the power system cope with busy hours. People need fair payment and protection against unsafe or unaffordable participation.
consequences: Lower peak demand can reduce some electricity costs.
Reliable flexibility can reduce outage risk when supply is tight.
Households and businesses can take part where the programme suits their needs.

planet.summary: Moving flexible electricity use can make better use of existing low-emissions supply. Benefits depend on what generation and equipment are actually avoided.
consequences: Fossil plants used mainly at busy hours may run less.
More available cleaner electricity can be used.
Some extra power plants or network capacity may become unnecessary.

economy.hiddenCost: Changing electricity use can save costs, but badly designed programs can make homes uncomfortable or unsafe.
economy.whoPays: People with flexible equipment may benefit more than households unable to shift essential use.
economy.physicalLimit: Some activities can move to another time. Medical equipment and other essential needs may not be flexible.
economy.defaultDriver: Some activities can move to another time. Medical equipment and other essential needs may not be flexible.
systemLevers: Protect essential use, allow people to opt out and reward useful verified changes.
Combine suitable automation with efficient appliances and help for households facing high bills.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Finding gas leaks helps only when operators fix them and confirm the repair. This can reduce wasted gas and some harmful pollution near facilities.
consequences: Repairs may reduce hazardous substances released alongside the gas.
Less saleable fuel is lost into the air.
Measuring the gas helps local people and public agencies find leaks they cannot see.

planet.summary: Verified repairs stop some releases of a powerful heat-trapping gas. Detection by itself does not deliver the reduction.
consequences: Successful repairs reduce near-term warming pressure.
Measurements make fossil-system releases easier to check.
Large leaks can be prioritised for quicker repair.

economy.hiddenCost: Finding leaks costs money and has little benefit if operators do not repair them.
economy.whoPays: Operators pay for inspections and repairs, with costs and saved fuel affecting customers and investors.
economy.physicalLimit: Detection depends on instruments, weather and leak size. A scan can miss releases occurring at another time.
economy.defaultDriver: Detection depends on instruments, weather and leak size. A scan can miss releases occurring at another time.
systemLevers: Use ground, aircraft or satellite observations together to target inspections.
Require prompt repairs and follow-up measurements showing the release has stopped.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Cooling equipment can use gases with less climate impact while continuing to protect people from heat. Safe installation, repair and recovery of old gases are essential.
consequences: People can retain access to cooling with fewer heat-trapping releases.
Training and proper servicing can improve technician safety.
Preventing leaks can reduce equipment problems and household losses.

planet.summary: Changing cooling gases and managing leaks can reduce powerful heat-trapping releases. Old equipment and discarded gas also need careful handling.
consequences: Lower-impact gases can reduce emissions from each leak.
Good servicing and recovery reduce losses over equipment lifetimes.
Efficient cooling can meet growing heat needs with less energy.

economy.hiddenCost: Replacing cooling gases can require new equipment, technician training and safe recovery of old gases.
economy.whoPays: Households and businesses face upgrade costs. Targeted support can help people unable to afford them.
economy.physicalLimit: Alternatives must match equipment and safety needs, including pressure and flammability.
economy.defaultDriver: Alternatives must match equipment and safety needs, including pressure and flammability.
systemLevers: Train technicians and check leaks during use and when equipment is retired.
Pair lower-warming gases with efficient cooling so electricity use does not erase the gains.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Taking carbon dioxide out of the air may help address a limited share of emissions that are difficult to eliminate. The benefit depends on verified, lasting storage and the resources used.
consequences: Reliable projects can address some remaining emissions alongside large emissions cuts.
Long-term monitoring and care can create skilled work.
Carefully designed land-based projects may also help damaged ecosystems recover.

planet.summary: Removing carbon dioxide can help only when storage lasts and the project avoids creating comparable new emissions. Methods have different land, water and energy demands.
consequences: Verified additional removal lowers the amount left in the air.
Some carefully designed land-based methods can improve soils or habitats.
A limited amount can balance emissions that remain difficult to eliminate.

economy.hiddenCost: Removing carbon from air can require energy, land or water. Costs and storage risks differ widely between methods.
economy.whoPays: Project buyers, public budgets and nearby communities may share costs and land or resource tradeoffs.
economy.physicalLimit: The climate benefit depends on how much is removed after project emissions and how long it stays stored.
economy.defaultDriver: The climate benefit depends on how much is removed after project emissions and how long it stays stored.
systemLevers: Measure removal and storage separately from emissions cuts.
Require lasting storage and clear monitoring, and avoid using uncertain future removal to delay direct cuts.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Buildings that need less energy can be cheaper and more comfortable to use. Good design also helps keep people safer during hot or cold periods.
consequences: Lower energy use can reduce bills and exposure to price rises.
Suitable upgrades can keep indoor temperatures safer for longer.
Ventilation and other well-designed improvements can support better indoor conditions.

planet.summary: Using less energy for the same building services can reduce fuel use and the equipment needed to supply it.
consequences: Electricity and heating-fuel demand can fall.
Efficient buildings can reduce demand during the busiest hours.
Lower demand can limit the need for additional generation and networks.

economy.hiddenCost: Upgrades cost money upfront, and poor work can fail to deliver expected savings.
economy.whoPays: Owners may pay for work while tenants receive the savings, or costs may be passed into rents. Support should account for both.
economy.physicalLimit: Results depend on the building, installation quality and how equipment is used.
economy.defaultDriver: Results depend on the building, installation quality and how equipment is used.
systemLevers: Set useful building and appliance standards and fund improvements in high-cost homes.
Check actual energy use and comfort after work is completed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Efficient electric equipment can provide both heating and cooling. Costs and benefits depend on the building, electricity prices and installation quality.
consequences: Well-suited systems can lower heating costs in efficient buildings.
Replacing fuel-burning furnaces removes that source of indoor combustion pollution.
Systems that provide cooling can help during dangerous heat.

planet.summary: Efficient electric heating reduces direct fuel burning in buildings. Its climate benefit increases as electricity becomes cleaner.
consequences: Less fossil fuel is burned at the building.
Moving heat can provide heating and cooling efficiently.
Power made with less fossil fuel reduces the heat-trapping gases released when this equipment runs.

economy.hiddenCost: Equipment, electrical upgrades and home improvements can cost more initially. Running costs depend on efficiency and electricity prices.
economy.whoPays: Owners, tenants and support programs may share costs. Renters need protection against unfair increases.
economy.physicalLimit: Performance depends on climate, equipment sizing, installation and how well the building holds heat.
economy.defaultDriver: Performance depends on climate, equipment sizing, installation and how well the building holds heat.
systemLevers: Match systems to local conditions and improve insulation or electrical supply where needed.
Use efficient equipment and targeted financial support, especially for households with limited income.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Insulation, draught repairs and other building upgrades can make indoor conditions safer with less energy. The work needs to suit local weather and maintain healthy ventilation.
consequences: Reduced energy needs can lower household bills.
Indoor temperatures may remain safe for longer during outages.
Properly designed repairs can reduce draughts, damp, mould and smoke entering from outside.

planet.summary: Improving existing buildings can reduce the energy needed to keep them comfortable. Lasting upgrades can also extend their useful life.
consequences: Heating and cooling demand can fall.
Lower demand during extremes can ease pressure on the grid.
Maintaining existing buildings can reduce the need for replacement construction.

economy.hiddenCost: Poorly planned sealing or insulation can create moisture or indoor-air problems despite reducing energy use.
economy.whoPays: Homeowners and public programs often pay upfront. Renters need access to benefits and protection from unfair rent rises.
economy.physicalLimit: A building still needs safe ventilation and suitable moisture control after gaps are sealed.
economy.defaultDriver: A building still needs safe ventilation and suitable moisture control after gaps are sealed.
systemLevers: Prioritize poorly performing homes and check materials, ventilation and installation quality.
Coordinate insulation and sealing with heating or cooling upgrades.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Shade, ventilation and suitable building materials can reduce indoor heat without relying entirely on air conditioning. They work within the limits of local weather and building design.
consequences: Lower indoor heat can reduce dangerous exposure.
Less powered cooling can lower bills and vulnerability to power cuts.
Shaded public spaces can make neighbourhoods more comfortable.

planet.summary: Designs that limit heat gain can reduce demand for powered cooling. Some also add vegetation when that suits the location.
consequences: Less electricity is needed to maintain comfortable temperatures.
Peak demand during hot hours can fall.
Suitable green spaces can provide habitat alongside shade.

economy.hiddenCost: Shade, reflective surfaces and ventilation need appropriate design and maintenance. Some options use land or water.
economy.whoPays: Building owners and public programs can fund improvements. Access should include renters and exposed neighbourhoods.
economy.physicalLimit: Ventilation may be unsuitable during smoke or when outdoor air is very hot or humid. Design must fit the place.
economy.defaultDriver: Ventilation may be unsuitable during smoke or when outdoor air is very hot or humid. Design must fit the place.
systemLevers: Include suitable shade and cool roofs in buildings and public spaces.
Protect indoor air quality and assess humidity, security and maintenance alongside cooling.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Rules based on real building performance can encourage owners to improve inefficient buildings. Funding and practical delivery determine whether residents benefit.
consequences: Predictable upgrade programmes can support skilled jobs.
Successful improvements can lower running costs and improve comfort.
Published performance makes poor-performing buildings easier to identify.

planet.summary: Rules tied to measured performance can reduce building energy use when owners deliver effective upgrades.
consequences: Actual energy use and operating emissions can fall.
Standards can encourage efficiency and cleaner heating.
Measured results make it easier to check whether promised reductions occurred.

economy.hiddenCost: Meeting new requirements may need major upgrades. Costs can reach tenants unless financing and protections are included.
economy.whoPays: Owners, public programs and occupants may share costs and savings unevenly.
economy.physicalLimit: Targets must reflect measured performance, building conditions and available upgrade methods.
economy.defaultDriver: Targets must reflect measured performance, building conditions and available upgrade methods.
systemLevers: Phase in clear targets with technical and financial support.
Track real outcomes and protect tenants from displacement or unfair cost increases.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Frequent and affordable shared transport can help people reach work, school and services without a private car. Benefits depend on useful routes and reliable service.
consequences: Some households can spend less on daily travel.
People unable to drive gain another way to reach essential destinations.
Replacing car journeys can reduce roadside pollution and traffic risks.

planet.summary: Reliable shared transport can reduce fuel use and space needed for private vehicles. The benefit depends on replacing car journeys and supporting useful development patterns.
consequences: Less driving can reduce transport emissions.
Homes and services can be built closer together around good routes.
Demand for roads and parking can fall.

economy.hiddenCost: New routes need continuing funds for reliable service and maintenance, as well as construction.
economy.whoPays: Public budgets, fares and other funding share costs. Benefits depend on who can afford and reach the service.
economy.physicalLimit: A route helps only if it connects useful destinations at suitable times with safe, accessible stops.
economy.defaultDriver: A route helps only if it connects useful destinations at suitable times with safe, accessible stops.
systemLevers: Fund frequent, dependable service and safe links to homes, jobs and schools.
Keep fares affordable and prevent improvements from forcing existing residents out.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Safe, connected walking and cycling routes make short trips easier without a motor vehicle. The network needs to work for the people and journeys it serves.
consequences: More daily journeys can include physical activity.
Households may spend less on transport.
Well-designed streets can become quieter and safer.

planet.summary: Safe walking and cycling routes can avoid fuel use on short trips. Connected routes also support places where daily destinations are closer together.
consequences: Replacing motor journeys reduces fuel demand.
Less car use can reduce pressure for roads and parking.
Compact development can use land more efficiently.

economy.hiddenCost: Walking and cycling routes need maintenance and protection from traffic, heat and pollution.
economy.whoPays: Public budgets usually fund networks. Benefits depend on accessibility for different ages and abilities.
economy.physicalLimit: A disconnected or unsafe section can make an otherwise useful route unusable.
economy.defaultDriver: A disconnected or unsafe section can make an otherwise useful route unusable.
systemLevers: Build continuous protected links to everyday destinations and public transport.
Provide safe crossings, shade, accessible design and regular maintenance.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Vehicles powered by batteries remove exhaust from the journeys they replace. They can reduce fuel costs, while tyres, roads and electricity production still have impacts.
consequences: People near streets can face less tailpipe pollution.
Drivers are less exposed to oil-price changes.
Running and maintenance costs can fall, depending on the vehicle and electricity prices.

planet.summary: Electric vehicles reduce oil use, with larger climate benefits as their power supply becomes cleaner. Battery and vehicle production remain part of the full impact.
consequences: Emissions over a vehicle's life can fall with cleaner charging.
Less petroleum is needed for driving.
Managed charging can help match electricity demand with available supply.

economy.hiddenCost: Vehicles still need materials and road space, and tyres still release particles. Batteries and chargers add costs.
economy.whoPays: Buyers, electricity users and public programs share costs. People without private parking need access to charging.
economy.physicalLimit: Benefits depend on vehicle size, manufacturing, electricity supply and lifetime use.
economy.defaultDriver: Benefits depend on vehicle size, manufacturing, electricity supply and lifetime use.
systemLevers: Improve charging and cleaner electricity together, with battery repair and recycling.
Support smaller vehicles and reliable public transport alongside replacing fossil-fuel cars.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Using less emissions-intensive cement can reduce the climate impact of essential construction. Building design and material choice determine the benefit.
consequences: Infrastructure can be built with fewer production emissions.
New materials can support demand for skilled industrial work.
Designs needing less concrete can save raw materials as well as emissions.

planet.summary: Changes in cement ingredients, fuel and material use can reduce construction emissions. The method must still meet safe performance requirements.
consequences: Less limestone processing and fuel burning can reduce carbon dioxide releases.
Material-saving designs can reduce demand for new raw materials.
Suitable industrial by-products may replace some ingredients when strong safeguards are met.

economy.hiddenCost: Different materials or equipment may cost more and need testing before builders can use them confidently.
economy.whoPays: Producers, builders, public projects and buyers can share the initial cost.
economy.physicalLimit: Materials must meet strength and durability needs. Suitable ingredients and carbon-capture infrastructure are not available everywhere.
economy.defaultDriver: Materials must meet strength and durability needs. Suitable ingredients and carbon-capture infrastructure are not available everywhere.
systemLevers: Allow verified lower-emissions materials in building rules and public purchasing.
Require clear product-level emissions information as well as performance testing.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Cleaner steel production can keep supplying an important material while reducing pollution. Workers and regions need support as plants and skills change.
consequences: Essential industrial capacity can continue with fewer harmful releases.
Recycling, cleaner power and new production methods create demand for different skills.
Lower emissions may reduce exposure to future charges for carbon pollution.

planet.summary: Cleaner steelmaking can reduce coal use and carbon dioxide releases. Recycling and efficient design can lower demand for new material as well.
consequences: Lower-emissions production can replace coal-based processes.
Good-quality scrap becomes more useful for new steel.
Efficient use can reduce the amount of primary metal required.

economy.hiddenCost: New plants or conversions require large investment and may change local jobs and energy demand.
economy.whoPays: Producers, buyers, public budgets and industrial communities share costs and benefits.
economy.physicalLimit: Available cleaner electricity, hydrogen, scrap quality and plant design determine which routes work.
economy.defaultDriver: Available cleaner electricity, hydrogen, scrap quality and plant design determine which routes work.
systemLevers: Plan clean power and other needed infrastructure alongside factory changes.
Create credible demand through purchasing standards and support workers during conversion.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Repairing damaged habitats can support people who depend on healthy land and water. Benefits depend on lasting recovery and care.
consequences: Farming, fishing and other local livelihoods may gain from healthier ecosystems.
Some projects reduce flooding, heat, erosion or water-quality risks.
Restored places can regain cultural, recreational and community value.

planet.summary: Repairing damaged ecosystems can rebuild habitat and the processes that support it. Lasting benefits require the original pressures to be reduced.
consequences: Plants and animals can regain connected places to live.
Healthier soils and vegetation can store carbon and help regulate water.
More resilient habitats can recover better from some climate stresses.

economy.hiddenCost: Poor projects can displace people, plant unsuitable species or claim carbon benefits that do not last.
economy.whoPays: Landholders, communities and public or private funders share costs. Rights and access need protection.
economy.physicalLimit: Recovery depends on removing the original pressure and maintaining suitable habitat under a changing climate.
economy.defaultDriver: Recovery depends on removing the original pressure and maintaining suitable habitat under a changing climate.
systemLevers: Protect remaining healthy ecosystems and restore suitable native variety on damaged land.
Respect Indigenous and community rights and fund long-term care and monitoring.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Useful warnings give people time to prepare before danger arrives. They protect people only when alerts reach them and practical action is possible.
consequences: Timely preparation can reduce injuries and deaths.
Households and services can protect people and important supplies earlier.
Shared plans help weather, health and emergency teams work with communities.

planet.summary: Early warnings can give people time to prevent additional environmental damage during emergencies. They do not remove the underlying hazard.
consequences: Preparation can reduce avoidable spills or damage from an unmanaged emergency.
Earlier action may protect sensitive habitats and essential facilities.
Monitoring can reveal when several hazards are developing together.

economy.hiddenCost: Forecasting equipment and messages need continuing funding. An accurate alert has limited value without practical help to act.
economy.whoPays: Public agencies and communities need resources for communication, safe transport and shelter.
economy.physicalLimit: Warnings can fail to reach people or arrive without enough time, trust or means to respond.
economy.defaultDriver: Warnings can fail to reach people or arrive without enough time, trust or means to respond.
systemLevers: Design messages with exposed communities, in accessible formats and local languages.
Connect alerts to funded evacuation, shelter, health and essential-service plans.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: A funded city plan can turn heat forecasts into practical protection. It needs to reach people whose homes, work or health leave them most exposed.
consequences: Early action can reduce preventable heat illness and deaths.
Workers, older people, children and people without safe cooling may receive targeted support.
Health services, utilities, employers and housing teams can coordinate their response.

planet.summary: Heat plans can support long-term changes that keep cities cooler. Environmental benefits depend on including measures beyond emergency air conditioning.
consequences: Shade and suitable building design can reduce sudden peaks in cooling demand.
Greener public spaces can provide cooler surroundings.
Local observations can help direct future heat-reduction work.

economy.hiddenCost: A plan needs staff, outreach, transport and safe places to cool down. Writing the plan alone does not protect people.
economy.whoPays: Local agencies, employers and service providers share responsibilities. Support should reach people facing the greatest exposure.
economy.physicalLimit: Protection depends on timely action, accessible services and conditions inside homes and workplaces.
economy.defaultDriver: Protection depends on timely action, accessible services and conditions inside homes and workplaces.
systemLevers: Set local alert triggers and clear responsibilities, backed by budgets.
Protect workers and invest in shade, cooler buildings and accessible cooling during emergencies.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Affordable, reliable ways to stay cool can protect people during dangerous heat. Access must include those unable to buy or operate cooling on their own.
consequences: Safe indoor temperatures can reduce heat illness and deaths.
People with health conditions can receive protection when heat is especially risky.
Households may avoid choosing between a manageable bill and a safe temperature.

planet.summary: Safe cooling can be provided with less environmental pressure when efficient equipment and better buildings are part of the programme.
consequences: Efficient systems reduce electricity demand and the need for cooling gases.
Insulation and shade limit unnecessary energy use.
Ways of cooling without powered equipment reduce dependence on air conditioning.

economy.hiddenCost: More cooling can raise electricity demand, bills and gas leakage if equipment and supply are poorly planned.
economy.whoPays: Households need affordable running costs as well as affordable equipment. Public support can target those with the fewest alternatives.
economy.physicalLimit: Cooling protection depends on reliable power, efficient equipment and access during the hottest periods.
economy.defaultDriver: Cooling protection depends on reliable power, efficient equipment and access during the hottest periods.
systemLevers: Combine efficient cooling with shade and suitable home improvements.
Provide targeted bill support and plans for outages and residents with medical needs.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Services designed and maintained for flooding are more likely to keep working during an event. Protection has limits and needs to match future conditions.
consequences: Water, power, transport and health services can suffer fewer interruptions.
Households may face fewer repeated losses and outages.
Avoided damage can reduce some recovery costs.

planet.summary: Well-designed flood protection can reduce pollution released when essential services fail. Designs that work with natural habitats can provide additional benefits.
consequences: Restoring wetlands or floodplains can create space for water and wildlife.
Protected sewage and chemical facilities are less likely to release pollution during floods.
Fewer infrastructure failures can limit damage to nearby waters.

economy.hiddenCost: Flood walls and drainage can move water problems elsewhere or encourage building behind defenses that can still fail.
economy.whoPays: Public budgets, owners and nearby communities share costs, including people downstream.
economy.physicalLimit: Every defense has a design limit and needs maintenance. Future floods may exceed past experience.
economy.defaultDriver: Every defense has a design limit and needs maintenance. Future floods may exceed past experience.
systemLevers: Use future conditions in design and protect natural flood-storage areas where suitable.
Combine engineered protection with land-use limits and avoid adding unsafe development.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Treating water so it can be used again can strengthen local supplies. Safety and benefit depend on suitable treatment and replacing demand on other sources.
consequences: A dependable local supply can become available for suitable uses.
Communities may be less exposed to drought or imported-water disruption.
Investment can improve wastewater treatment and reduce pollution.

planet.summary: Using treated water again can reduce pressure on rivers and groundwater when it replaces new withdrawals.
consequences: Less fresh water may need to be taken from natural sources.
Effective treatment can reduce polluted discharges.
Reduced withdrawals can leave more water for ecosystems.

economy.hiddenCost: Treatment needs energy and maintenance and can produce concentrated waste. Poor pricing can put useful water beyond some people's reach.
economy.whoPays: Utilities, customers and public funding share costs and benefits.
economy.physicalLimit: Required treatment depends on whether the water will be drunk, used on crops or used for another purpose.
economy.defaultDriver: Required treatment depends on whether the water will be drunk, used on crops or used for another purpose.
systemLevers: Match treatment to the intended use and monitor relevant contaminants.
Use efficient cleaner energy and protect affordability and water needed by rivers and habitats.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Farming adapted to local climate risks can make food and farm incomes more dependable. Measures need to suit the crop, soil and water available.
consequences: A mix of crops and better planning can reduce some harvest shocks.
Healthier soil can hold water better and reduce dependence on costly inputs.
Worker protection and more reliable production can support rural livelihoods.

planet.summary: Farming methods suited to local risks can protect soil and water while supporting production. Benefits depend on management and limits on total resource use.
consequences: Keeping soil covered can reduce erosion and nutrient losses.
Healthier soil and varied habitats can support stored carbon and wildlife.
More efficient water use reduces total pressure only when extra demand does not cancel the saving.

economy.hiddenCost: Changing practices can require equipment, training or temporary income support. Labels alone do not guarantee better results.
economy.whoPays: Farmers, workers, consumers and public programs may share the costs and benefits.
economy.physicalLimit: No single practice works in every soil and climate. Water use, yields, emissions and working conditions must be considered together.
economy.defaultDriver: No single practice works in every soil and climate. Water use, yields, emissions and working conditions must be considered together.
systemLevers: Fund locally tested practices and practical advice for farmers.
Reward measured improvements in soil, water and income, with emissions cuts and worker protection.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: A planned, supported move can reduce repeated exposure to dangerous or unaffordable hazards. Residents need a real role in decisions and a viable place to live.
consequences: Moving before a disaster can reduce repeated losses.
Planning creates time to arrange housing, land, schools and income.
Keeping communities together may be easier than after emergency displacement.

planet.summary: Moving development away from repeatedly hazardous areas can create room for natural recovery. The result depends on what happens to both the old site and the new one.
consequences: Floodplains or shorelines may regain space and habitat.
Less repeated rebuilding can reduce disturbance in exposed ecosystems.
Some vacated areas can support wetlands and other natural protection.

economy.hiddenCost: Moving can disrupt jobs, culture and community ties as well as cost money. A poorly run move can deepen existing hardship.
economy.whoPays: Residents, receiving communities and public programs need fair arrangements for land, housing and ongoing services.
economy.physicalLimit: A safer site is not enough without secure rights, income opportunities and community consent.
economy.defaultDriver: A safer site is not enough without secure rights, income opportunities and community consent.
systemLevers: Plan voluntary moves with affected communities before an emergency forces decisions.
Guarantee fair support, services and continued cultural ties, including funding for receiving communities.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Healthy habitats can help protect people from heat, waves, floods and erosion. Their protection depends on location, condition and continued care.
consequences: Trees, wetlands and coastal habitats can reduce some harmful exposure.
Projects can provide accessible green space and local work.
Suitable designs may improve water quality and neighbourhood comfort.

planet.summary: Using healthy habitats to reduce hazards can also support wildlife and natural processes. Native species, connected space and long-term care help these benefits last.
consequences: Damaged habitats can recover their functions.
Plants and soils may store more carbon.
Projects can reconnect separated landscapes and waterways.

economy.hiddenCost: Restored wetlands, trees or reefs need space and care. They may fail if pressure continues or future conditions become unsuitable.
economy.whoPays: Land users, local communities and public or private funders share costs and benefits.
economy.physicalLimit: Natural protection has limits and may take time to recover. It cannot make every exposed site safe.
economy.defaultDriver: Natural protection has limits and may take time to recover. It cannot make every exposed site safe.
systemLevers: Protect existing healthy ecosystems and monitor whether restoration is working.
Combine suitable natural protection with land-use limits and engineered measures where needed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: The benefits described depend on suitable design, funding and continued operation. Check results for the people and places the project is meant to help.

human.summary: Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve. A thinner freshwater reserve beneath an island can leave wells with less water or more salt. Making that supply safe to drink may become harder.
consequences: Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply. Saltier underground water gives utilities fewer easy-to-treat supplies. Extra treatment or replacement sources may be needed.

Heavy pumping can draw salty groundwater into wells. If that water is repeatedly used on fields, evaporation can leave salt around roots. This does not happen everywhere, especially where water stays fresh and drainage removes salts. Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living

planet.summary: Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve.
consequences: Pumping faster than water is replaced lowers underground reserves. Wells can then reach less water or stop working at their existing depth.
Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply.

economy.hiddenCost: Pumping water faster than it is replaced can lower well levels and, in some sediments, cause lasting ground sinking.
economy.whoPays: People with shallow wells may lose access first. Farmers, households and water utilities can face deeper pumping or replacement-supply costs.
economy.physicalLimit: Some fine-grained underground layers compact when pressure falls and cannot regain all their storage space. Not every underground water store behaves this way.
economy.defaultDriver: Cheap pumping and weak limits on total withdrawals can encourage taking more water than the system can replace.
systemLevers: Set withdrawals using evidence about recharge, connected rivers and essential needs.
Protect suitable recharge areas and reduce incentives for excessive pumping.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
consequences: Changes in when and how much river water arrives can make electricity from dams less dependable. Reservoirs and turbines may no longer receive the flow they were designed around.

Weaker or differently timed river flows provide less fresh water to resist the sea. Saltier water can then move farther upstream. Saltier water reaching drinking-water intakes can exceed normal treatment capabilities. Utilities may need to change intake locations, blend supplies or use additional treatment.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Weaker or differently timed river flows provide less fresh water to resist the sea. Saltier water can then move farther upstream.
consequences: A dam may receive water at different times or in different amounts than expected. Stored supplies can then become less predictable under existing operating rules.
Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: Keep earlier approved values when updates are missing. Clearly identify provisional readings, absent data and temporary limits on access to the source.
economy.defaultDriver: Warming changes evaporation, precipitation and the timing of snowmelt. These can alter how much water rivers carry and when it arrives.
systemLevers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.

planet.summary: Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.

economy.hiddenCost: Sediment can take up space intended for water, while changing inflows make stored supplies less dependable.
economy.whoPays: Water users, power operators and public budgets may face lost supply, repairs or sediment-removal costs.
economy.physicalLimit: Usable storage depends on sediment, water levels and the location of outlets. The reservoir may lose useful capacity before it appears full of sediment.
economy.defaultDriver: Erosion upstream and changing rainfall can add pressure to reservoirs designed for older conditions.
systemLevers: Reduce avoidable soil erosion upstream and monitor usable storage.
Choose sediment-management methods suited to the dam and downstream river, alongside better inflow planning.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Limited stored water or restrictions on releases can leave less water available to turn turbines. Electricity from the dam then becomes less dependable.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Changes in stored water and release timing can affect downstream flows. Effects on habitats depend on how the reservoir is operated and the water needs of the river.
domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established

economy.hiddenCost: A reservoir can remain on the map while supplying less dependable water, electricity or flood protection.
economy.whoPays: Water and power providers, farmers and people farther down the river may face limits on supply. They may need backup power or urgent changes to how they use water.
economy.physicalLimit: Enough usable water must be available at the right time. Low storage, sediment and poorly timed inflows can prevent expected releases.
economy.defaultDriver: Older operating rules may no longer fit changing rainfall and snowmelt.
systemLevers: Update release rules using present conditions and a range of future inflows.
Coordinate water supply, electricity and flood planning across the river basin.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily. A surge of fast-moving water can wash material away from around a bridge's supports. Losing that material can weaken the foundations.
consequences: Earlier melting moves snow-fed river flows toward an earlier part of the year. Less may remain for the warm season unless storage or rainfall makes up the difference. Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.

Earlier or faster melting adds water inside mountain snow. Slopes may become unstable when wet layers lose their strength. Avalanches can bury or damage roads, railways, power lines and communications equipment. Repeated closures are especially disruptive where few alternative mountain routes exist.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily.
consequences: Earlier melting moves snow-fed river flows toward an earlier part of the year. Less may remain for the warm season unless storage or rainfall makes up the difference.
Earlier or faster melting adds water inside mountain snow. Slopes may become unstable when wet layers lose their strength.
domains: ice, snow, frozen ground, and albedo

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: Missing observations do not mean no change. Snow, glaciers, sea ice and ice sheets must not be combined as if their quantities were interchangeable.
economy.defaultDriver: Darkened snow absorbs more sunlight than clean snow. This can make melting begin sooner or proceed faster in the affected area.
systemLevers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Very dry soil leaves roots unable to obtain enough water. Crop growth and harvests can suffer, with effects that vary between crops and seasons.
consequences: Very dry soil provides little cooling through evaporation. More energy heats the land and air, reinforcing hot, dry conditions above the ground. Strong drying conditions increase plants' water demand. Plants may close tiny leaf openings to conserve water, which can reduce growth and make harvests less reliable.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living

planet.summary: When soil becomes very dry, farmers may pump more underground water for irrigation. Added pumping can lower well levels where replacement water is insufficient.
consequences: Very dry soil provides little cooling through evaporation. More energy heats the land and air, reinforcing hot, dry conditions above the ground.

economy.hiddenCost: Very dry soil can reduce harvests and increase erosion. Recovery may require extra water, soil protection or changes in planting.
economy.whoPays: Farmers lose income, while workers and food buyers can face wider effects if production falls.
economy.physicalLimit: Plants cannot use all water held in soil. The point at which roots cannot draw enough depends on the soil, crop and conditions.
economy.defaultDriver: Low rainfall, heat and poor soil management can combine to reduce water available to roots.
systemLevers: Monitor root-zone moisture and use planting and water plans suited to local conditions.
Keep suitable ground cover and protect organic matter without increasing unsustainable water demand.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Rapid floods can wash dirt and pollution into water sources or damage intakes. Treatment plants may need extra cleaning steps or temporary interruptions.
consequences: Flooding can leave standing water, damage drains and change how people store water. In some places, this creates more breeding sites for mosquitoes and increases contact with people.
Sudden floods can contaminate drinking-water facilities and spread harmful germs. Effective treatment and hygiene can prevent exposure from becoming an outbreak.

planet.summary: Fast-rising floodwater can exceed the capacity of sewers and treatment plants. Used water can then back up or escape into surrounding areas.
consequences: Rapid floods can wash dirt and pollution into water sources or damage intakes. Treatment plants may need extra cleaning steps or temporary interruptions.
Sudden floods can contaminate drinking-water facilities and spread harmful germs. Effective treatment and hygiene can prevent exposure from becoming an outbreak.

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: Missing data do not mean no flow, no water use or no impact. A result for an entire river basin cannot be applied directly to one building or household.
economy.defaultDriver: Intense rain can arrive faster than the ground can absorb it or drains and rivers can carry it away. Water can then rise quickly and flood nearby areas.
systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Lower water volumes during drought can leave salts and pollutants more concentrated. Utilities may need more treatment to provide safe drinking water.
consequences: A long drought reduces water reaching dams and may lower stored water levels. Less dependable flow means less dependable electricity generation.
Long dry periods reduce river supplies and the water replenishing underground reserves. Shortages become more likely if demand stays high.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: A long drought reduces river flow and the flushing of river mouths. Saltier water can move farther inland and remain there longer.
consequences: A long dry period can keep incoming river water low. Reservoirs may fail to refill enough to meet later needs.
Lower water volumes during drought can leave salts and pollutants more concentrated. Utilities may need more treatment to provide safe drinking water.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: Require all twelve monthly values before publishing an event. Missing months are not drought-free. Clearly mark events cut off at a year boundary.
economy.defaultDriver: A long-lasting high-pressure pattern can divert storms and keep rain away from the same region. Dry conditions can then continue for longer.
systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: A shallow store of fresh groundwater can become less useful when saltwater squeezes into it. Communities may need more expensive and less dependable alternatives.
consequences: Water may still be present but too salty to use without treatment.
Households and utilities may pay more for storage, imported water or removal of salt.
Farms and daily water access become more vulnerable where few other sources exist.

planet.summary: A thinner freshwater reserve beneath an island can leave wells with less water or more salt. Making that supply safe to drink may become harder.

economy.hiddenCost: Small islands may need more expensive treatment or imported water when shallow underground supplies become salty.
economy.whoPays: Island households, farmers and utilities can face extra costs and less reliable access.
economy.physicalLimit: The freshwater layer depends on rainfall, pumping and surrounding seawater. Small changes can matter where the layer is thin.
economy.defaultDriver: Sea-level changes, drought and heavy pumping can reduce the thickness of usable freshwater.
systemLevers: Monitor well levels and salt content and limit pumping accordingly.
Use suitable rainwater collection and storage to reduce pressure on underground supplies.

human.summary: Water may remain available while becoming harder to make safe. Utilities and households can face higher costs and less reliable service.
consequences: Changing contamination or salt levels can require more complex treatment or different intakes.
People may face higher bills, boil-water notices or interrupted service.
Small systems with limited funding can struggle to respond to sudden changes.

planet.summary: Difficulties treating water mainly describe a service problem. Environmental effects depend on the original contamination and any treatment or waste changes, rather than treatment cost alone.

economy.hiddenCost: Salt, mud, algae or other contamination can increase the cost of making water safe. A plant may struggle even while it remains open.
economy.whoPays: Water customers and utilities face the bill, with small systems and low-income households often having fewer alternatives.
economy.physicalLimit: Each plant can treat only certain amounts and types of contamination. Some changes require different equipment or another water source.
economy.defaultDriver: Floods, drought and salt intrusion can make source water less predictable than the plant was designed for.
systemLevers: Improve monitoring and treatment for the contaminants actually present.
Provide backup sources or links between systems, with support for places lacking spare capacity.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Without forest cover, more soil can wash into streams supplying drinking water. Dirtier and less predictable source water can make treatment harder and more costly.
consequences: Forest damage can change when water reaches a dam and how much sediment it carries. These changes can make electricity generation less reliable.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Losing trees around rivers can increase erosion and change water flow and habitat. Severe or repeated damage can reduce the ability of freshwater communities to survive and recover.
consequences: Without forest cover, more soil can wash into streams supplying drinking water. Dirtier and less predictable source water can make treatment harder and more costly.
Forest loss can increase erosion, change river channels and remove streamside habitat. Some stretches may become unsuitable, separating populations along the river.

economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: An unsurveyed habitat is unknown, not empty or healthy. Finding a species, counting its numbers, assessing habitat condition and establishing extinction require different evidence.
economy.defaultDriver: Heat and drying can strain forests in river catchments. Greater water loss and fire risk can damage trees and change how water moves through the area.
systemLevers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Overflowing sewage systems can expose people to water carrying harmful germs. Outbreak risk rises when treatment and sanitation no longer contain that exposure.
consequences: When sewers or treatment plants cannot handle the incoming water, emergency releases may bypass normal cleaning steps. The released water may be untreated or only partly treated. Releasing used water without normal treatment can add pollutants and suspended dirt to a river. Water plants downstream may need extra work and expense to make supplies safe.

planet.summary: When sewers or treatment plants cannot handle the incoming water, emergency releases may bypass normal cleaning steps. The released water may be untreated or only partly treated.
consequences: Where rainwater and sewage share a pipe system, too much incoming water can escape through an overflow outlet. This connection applies only to systems built to carry both together.
Overflowing sewage systems can expose people to water carrying harmful germs. Outbreak risk rises when treatment and sanitation no longer contain that exposure.

economy.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: Missing data do not mean no flow, no water use or no impact. A result for an entire river basin cannot be applied directly to one building or household.
economy.defaultDriver: Fast-rising floodwater can exceed the capacity of sewers and treatment plants. Used water can then back up or escape into surrounding areas.
systemLevers: More storage, treatment capacity and protection from floodwater can reduce sewage overflows. Separating rainwater from sewage flows can also ease pressure on the system.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Releasing used water without normal treatment can add pollutants and suspended dirt to a river. Water plants downstream may need extra work and expense to make supplies safe.
consequences: Used water released without normal treatment can add nutrients that feed algae. Harmful growth is more likely where warmth, slow flushing and suitable species also occur. Toxic algae or low oxygen can kill fish or make seafood unsafe. Harvest closures and damaged stocks can then interrupt supplies arriving at ports and markets.

Untreated water can add nutrients and decaying material near the coast. Breaking down that material uses oxygen and can contribute to shortages for marine animals. Low oxygen can kill target species or push them away from fishing grounds. Local catches then become less reliable.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living

Upgrade pumps and treatment where needed and use monitoring to manage large inflows.

human.summary: Irrigation that needs more pumping for the same harvest can drain underground reserves. The effect depends on how much of the extra water returns as usable groundwater. Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.
consequences: Poorly managed irrigation and drainage can leave dissolved salts around plant roots. Salty groundwater rising toward the surface can add to the build-up. Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.

Water lost before it benefits crops may be replaced by extra pumping. Underground reserves decline if withdrawals keep exceeding refill and usable return flows. Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living

planet.summary: Water lost before it benefits crops may be replaced by extra pumping. Underground reserves decline if withdrawals keep exceeding refill and usable return flows.
consequences: Poorly used irrigation water can require more pumping for the same harvest. This can lower well supplies where underground water is not replaced quickly enough.
Irrigation that needs more pumping for the same harvest can drain underground reserves. The effect depends on how much of the extra water returns as usable groundwater.

Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

economy.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.
economy.physicalLimit: Keep the latest reviewed period and show its age when updates stop. Missing generation, capacity or consumption does not mean zero.
economy.defaultDriver: Limited stored water or restrictions on releases can leave less water available to turn turbines. Electricity from the dam then becomes less dependable.
systemLevers: Plan electricity supply, networks and demand together so cleaner options remain dependable.
Improve efficiency and maintain equipment, with backup arrangements suited to essential services and local hazards.

human.summary: When water-sharing agreements fail, disputes can become harder to settle. Escalation depends on institutions and wider political conditions. Violence is not inevitable.
domains: housing, support after moving and public services

domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established

economy.hiddenCost: Damage to housing and repeated disruption can create repair, temporary accommodation and moving costs. The burden depends on insurance, public support and safe alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Residents, landlords, insurers and public services may share the bill. People with little savings or secure housing can have fewer recovery options.
economy.physicalLimit: A physical hazard does not prove a social outcome occurred. Missing administrative records do not mean no cases.
economy.defaultDriver: Changes in river flow can make older water-sharing rules difficult to follow. Agreements based on historical supplies may no longer match the water available.
systemLevers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.
Fund practical support and monitor who can actually access it, especially where people have few alternatives.

human.summary: Removing salt from water uses electricity. Heavy reliance on this process can add energy costs, with household effects depending on prices and support.
consequences: Salt-removal plants need energy to provide water. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, operating the plants adds carbon dioxide releases. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Salt-removal plants need energy to provide water. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, operating the plants adds carbon dioxide releases.

economy.hiddenCost: Removing salt from seawater adds electricity, equipment and waste-management costs to water supply.
economy.whoPays: Customers and public budgets pay for plants and operation. The burden depends on pricing and support for essential use.
economy.physicalLimit: Separating salt and water always needs energy. Actual use depends on salt content, equipment and how much water is recovered.
economy.defaultDriver: Shortages or salty groundwater can make coastal areas increasingly reliant on energy-intensive replacement supplies.
systemLevers: Compare conservation, treated-water reuse and salt removal within one water plan.
Use efficient treatment and cleaner power while managing concentrated salty waste and affordability.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Water from melting ice sheets raises the sea's starting level. Coastal flooding then depends on local tides, storms, land movement and the people or buildings exposed. Flooding from the sea can add salt and other contamination to drinking-water sources or disrupt intakes. Water plants may then have difficulty providing safe supplies.
consequences: Ice loss and related changes to coasts and frozen ground can threaten polar buildings and transport. The risk is greatest where facilities depend on stable ice or land. Damage to roads, power lines or utilities in remote polar areas can interrupt essential services. Difficult access and limited alternatives can make recovery harder.

Losing ice can change where meltwater collects and how it drains. Flood hazards depend on whether water becomes trapped, how it escapes and what lies downstream. Sudden releases of stored glacier water can produce river flows far above seasonal levels. Repeated releases change the timing, size and sediment carried by downstream floods.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Meltwater from Antarctic ice makes nearby seawater fresher and less dense. This can reduce the formation of water that sinks to the deepest ocean.
consequences: Faster ice movement and ice loss can be signs that floating ice is providing less support to ice inland. These observations need local evidence to identify the cause. Ice loss alone does not explain every change.
Losing ice can change where meltwater collects and how it drains. Flood hazards depend on whether water becomes trapped, how it escapes and what lies downstream.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life

economy.physicalLimit: Do not mix glacier totals with ice-sheet totals. Different time periods can be combined only if uncertainty and shared errors are handled explicitly.
economy.defaultDriver: Warmer air melts ice at the surface, while warmer seawater can thin floating ice around the edges. Reduced support can also let ice on land flow into the sea faster.
systemLevers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

human.summary: A sudden glacier-lake flood can send fast, powerful flows past bridges. These can wash away the material supporting their foundations.
consequences: If a lake held beside a glacier breaks through its barrier, stored water can rush downstream. The flood can also carry large amounts of sediment. A surge of fast-moving water can wash material away from around a bridge's supports. Losing that material can weaken the foundations.

If ice or loose rock holding back a glacier lake fails, stored water can escape quickly. The flood can carry large amounts of water and sediment downstream. Sudden releases of stored glacier water can produce river flows far above seasonal levels. Repeated releases change the timing, size and sediment carried by downstream floods.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.
