human.summary: A longer ice-free season can allow vessels to use northern routes for more of the year. Moving ice, storms, ports, insurance and rules still determine whether traffic actually increases. More ships using Arctic routes means more journeys exposed to changing ice conditions. Remote locations and limited rescue or repair services can make disruptions harder to manage.
consequences: A shorter season of sea ice leaves Arctic coasts more exposed to waves and erosion. It can also shorten periods when people can safely use ice-based access routes. Damage to roads, power lines or utilities in remote polar areas can interrupt essential services. Difficult access and limited alternatives can make recovery harder.

A shorter ice season can leave thinner and less connected Arctic sea ice. Winds and currents can move this ice more readily through areas used by ships. Moving sea ice can enter planned ship routes and narrow safe passages. Ships may need to wait, change course or seek icebreaker support even when total ice cover is low.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Less time covered by bright sea ice leaves darker water exposed to sunlight for longer. More absorbed energy contributes to faster warming in the Arctic.
consequences: A shorter season of sea ice leaves Arctic coasts more exposed to waves and erosion. It can also shorten periods when people can safely use ice-based access routes.
A shorter ice season can leave thinner and less connected Arctic sea ice. Winds and currents can move this ice more readily through areas used by ships.

Repeated flooding by seawater can increase expected insurance losses. Insurers may raise prices, limit coverage or stop offering policies in exposed areas.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

consequences: A small winter snowpack stores less water for later in the year. This can make reservoir supplies harder to predict and manage. Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.

Less stored winter snow can make a river basin more dependent on glacier melt. Once that glacier contribution begins declining, late-season water supplies become more exposed. After a glacier basin passes its period of greatest meltwater supply, the contribution can decline over time. People and power systems relying on that water may face less dependable dry-season flows.

human.summary: As oxygen falls, sensitive animals may leave or die while more tolerant ones remain. This changes local feeding relationships and the habitat available. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.

Severely depleted fish stocks leave fewer fish available to catch. Ports and markets may then receive smaller or less reliable supplies.

Water arriving with less oxygen gives a shallow sea less protection against further oxygen loss. A smaller additional loss may then be enough to harm local marine life. Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.

human.summary: Changes in mountain forests can affect local resources, recreation and valued habitats. Human effects depend on which forest areas are lost and what communities rely on them for.

planet.summary: Lasting changes in mountain forests alter shelter, food and connections used by wildlife. Some species lose habitat while others benefit from openings or forest expansion, so population changes need separate evidence.

economy.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
economy.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.
economy.physicalLimit: One fire scar is not range contraction. Treeline movement alone does not establish overall forest loss, and warming can have opposite effects at cold and dry boundaries.
economy.defaultDriver: Warming can dry lower forest margins and prevent young trees from establishing, while allowing trees to grow higher where cold once limited them. Both boundaries and local moisture need to be checked before claiming the forest is shrinking overall.
systemLevers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: A strong, long-lasting stream of moist air can produce heavy rain or snow when mountains or fronts lift it. Without suitable lifting, direction or duration, it may mainly provide useful water rather than an extreme event. Very heavy rain can overwhelm airport drains and reduce visibility. Flights and ground operations may be delayed or cancelled.
consequences: Sustained rain from a band of moist air can sharply raise river flow, especially on wet ground or melting snow. Dry soil, reservoirs and shorter events can limit runoff and allow beneficial replenishment. Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: A strong, long-lasting stream of moist air can produce heavy rain or snow when mountains or fronts lift it. Without suitable lifting, direction or duration, it may mainly provide useful water rather than an extreme event.
consequences: Sustained rain from a band of moist air can sharply raise river flow, especially on wet ground or melting snow. Dry soil, reservoirs and shorter events can limit runoff and allow beneficial replenishment.

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: Compare matching detection methods. Not every moisture plume reaches land, and water-vapour transport alone does not establish flood damage.
economy.defaultDriver: Warmer air can carry more water vapour, allowing long bands of moist air to transport more water. This does not guarantee more events or stronger winds in every place, and historical trends depend on the available record.
systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Weaker east-to-west winds over the equatorial Pacific allow warm surface water to move east. This can reinforce warming in the central and eastern Pacific. Changes in Pacific ocean temperatures can bring heat, drought or flooding to farming regions. These conditions can damage harvests and interrupt food supplies.
consequences: Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions. Changes linked to unusually cool Pacific waters can bring destructive rain to some regions and drought to others. Harvests and fisheries may be affected in different ways across regions.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living

planet.summary: Weaker east-to-west winds over the equatorial Pacific allow warm surface water to move east. This can reinforce warming in the central and eastern Pacific.
consequences: Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions.
Changes in east-to-west tropical Pacific winds affect how surface water moves and how cold water rises from below. The direction of the wind change determines the response.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life

economy.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.
economy.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.
economy.physicalLimit: Missing periods are unknown, not neutral conditions. Do not mix different index definitions or treat a TULIP score as an observed climate reading.
economy.defaultDriver: The usual east-to-west winds near the equator in the Pacific becoming stronger or weaker than their seasonal pattern. These winds influence ocean surface water and tropical rainfall. The sign of the change matters: an unusual reading does not always mean weakening.
systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Damage to coastal habitats can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake. Carbon actually released must be counted separately from carbon that is no longer being absorbed. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

planet.summary: Damage to coastal habitats can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake. Carbon actually released must be counted separately from carbon that is no longer being absorbed.

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.
economy.physicalLimit: Habitat area cannot be converted directly to emissions without evidence about its carbon stores and the type of damage.
economy.defaultDriver: Losing seagrass removes plants that take up carbon and can expose carbon-rich seabed to erosion and decay. Stored carbon may then be lost.
systemLevers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere. When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere.

economy.hiddenCost: Service interruptions can bring repair costs, lost working time and spending on backup supplies. Wider losses depend on how long the interruption lasts and which activities rely on it.
economy.whoPays: Service operators, customers, workers and public budgets can share the costs. People without alternative services are more exposed to disruption.
economy.physicalLimit: Methane growth alone does not show a global decline in removal capacity. Compare matching lifetime definitions, and do not assign changes to one gas without checking the wider chemistry.
economy.defaultDriver: Removing methane from air uses highly reactive chemicals called hydroxyl radicals. More methane can use some of that capacity and stay longer, but other chemical and weather changes can increase removal instead.

human.summary: The protective layer high in the atmosphere filters harmful ultraviolet sunlight. Changes in that protection can affect exposure, but a seasonal polar measurement does not directly describe everyone's local risk.

planet.summary: Ozone absorbs energy and warms the upper atmosphere. Losing it can cool the affected layer, although carbon dioxide also causes cooling there and cold conditions can themselves encourage ozone loss.

economy.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
economy.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.
economy.physicalLimit: Upper-atmosphere ozone is different from ground-level pollution. Antarctica does not represent the whole globe. Leave the missing 1995 year missing, and do not explain one unusual season without chemical and weather evidence.
economy.defaultDriver: High in the atmosphere, sunlight breaks down certain gases and releases chemicals containing chlorine or bromine that destroy ozone. Cold polar clouds can speed the process, but gas levels alone do not predict each season's ozone loss.
systemLevers: Reducing ozone-damaging cooling gases lowers the future supply of reactive chlorine and bromine high in the atmosphere. Recovery is slow and uneven because old equipment, long gas lifetimes and weather still matter.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Some aircraft trails spread into thin ice clouds, changing reflected sunlight and escaping heat. Most disappear quickly, and their warming and cooling effects can partly offset each other. Cloud changes affect both sunlight reflected away and heat kept near Earth. The combined effect can warm or cool the planet, so the direction must be checked rather than assumed.
consequences: Persistent aircraft ice clouds both reflect sunlight and trap outgoing heat. The assessed global net effect is warming, but uncertainty is large and individual trails can have little effect or cause cooling depending on place and time. When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Some aircraft trails spread into thin ice clouds, changing reflected sunlight and escaping heat. Most disappear quickly, and their warming and cooling effects can partly offset each other.
consequences: Persistent aircraft ice clouds both reflect sunlight and trap outgoing heat. The assessed global net effect is warming, but uncertainty is large and individual trails can have little effect or cause cooling depending on place and time.

economy.defaultDriver: More flights create more opportunities for exhaust to form ice clouds at cruising height. Persistent trails form only in suitable cold, humid air. Flight numbers alone cannot predict them.
systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Coastal flooding can affect cable landing stations and their power or land connections. Shared locations increase the risk of several links failing together, while protection, backup power and separated routes can prevent disruption. Losing shared cable landing or power facilities can remove several communication paths at once. Essential services are less affected where traffic can switch to independent routes with enough spare capacity.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Seawater, river flow and heavy rain arriving together can change flooding and salt exposure near coasts. Effects on habitats depend on the mix, depth and duration of water.
domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established

economy.whoPays: Service operators, customers, workers and public budgets can share the costs. People without alternative services are more exposed to disruption.
economy.physicalLimit: Missing data do not mean no flow, no water use or no impact. A result for an entire river basin cannot be applied directly to one building or household.
economy.defaultDriver: Low-lying shores exposed to storm-driven seawater face greater danger when high tides, waves or river flow occur at the same time. The combined water can overwhelm drainage or protection.

human.summary: Fish moving across borders can change which fleets can reach them and challenge existing catch agreements. Shared surveys and flexible agreements can manage the change without conflict. Repeated confrontations or failed fishing agreements can worsen political tensions. Most disputes remain within negotiation, and existing tensions may cause fishing incidents rather than result from them.
domains: housing, support after moving and public services

planet.summary: Fish moving toward different temperatures or depths can change local food webs and overlap between species. Movement alone does not show whether total populations have grown or declined.
domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established

economy.hiddenCost: Damage to housing and repeated disruption can create repair, temporary accommodation and moving costs. The burden depends on insurance, public support and safe alternatives.
economy.whoPays: Residents, landlords, insurers and public services may share the bill. People with little savings or secure housing can have fewer recovery options.
economy.physicalLimit: Landings alone do not prove a climate cause. Do not mix stocks or seasons, or extend results outside the survey area without an explicit model.
economy.defaultDriver: Unusually hot seawater can move suitable habitat farther away, deeper or toward the poles. Some fish move, while others stay, adjust or return after the event.
systemLevers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

human.summary: Salt or other contamination in coastal groundwater can make wells less dependable. The amount of water underground may hide a decline in its usefulness.
consequences: Wells may still contain water that has become too salty for normal use.
Farms and utilities lose flexibility when a formerly reliable freshwater source deteriorates.
Communities may become more dependent on imported water or costly salt removal.

planet.summary: Saltier underground water gives utilities fewer easy-to-treat supplies. Extra treatment or replacement sources may be needed.

economy.hiddenCost: Underground water can remain present but become too salty to use without extra treatment or a replacement supply.
economy.whoPays: Well users, farmers and coastal utilities can face higher costs or lost access.
economy.physicalLimit: Recovery from salt contamination can be slow and depends on the underground geology and water flows.
economy.defaultDriver: Heavy pumping and seawater movement can worsen quality where management tracks only the quantity withdrawn.
systemLevers: Monitor salt levels as well as water levels and limit damaging withdrawals.
Plan alternative supplies before existing wells become unreliable.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Long-lasting difficulty obtaining enough food can push people to leave their homes. Jobs, conflict and other economic conditions also influence whether people move.
consequences: More people facing acute hunger increases demand for food assistance. Funding and access limits can leave part of that need unmet.
More people facing severe hunger increases the need for urgent food, nutrition and delivery support. Response services must expand quickly enough to meet it.
domains: housing, support after moving and public services

economy.physicalLimit: Keep the last reviewed release and show its age. A missing country-year is not zero hardship.
economy.defaultDriver: Unreliable harvests can reduce local food supplies and increase prices. Households may then find it harder to obtain enough nutritious food.
systemLevers: Connect useful warnings with accessible health services and practical protection for exposed people.
Improve access to safe housing, water or cooling where the documented exposure requires it.

human.summary: Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops. Toxic algae or low oxygen can kill fish or make seafood unsafe. Harvest closures and damaged stocks can then interrupt supplies arriving at ports and markets.
consequences: Nutrient-rich coastal water can increase food for some jellyfish and create conditions they tolerate well. The response depends on the species and local water conditions. Dense jellyfish groups can clog fishing nets, harm catches or affect fish-farm enclosures. Local fishing operations may be interrupted while the event lasts.

Extra nutrients can produce more algae in shallow seas. As this material decays, it can use oxygen faster than fresh water movement replaces it near the seabed. Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living

planet.summary: Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops.
consequences: Excess nutrients and organic matter can add stress to coastal reefs. This may make heat-related bleaching and recovery worse, depending on local conditions.
Extra nutrients can produce more algae in shallow seas. As this material decays, it can use oxygen faster than fresh water movement replaces it near the seabed.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life

human.summary: Extra daytime and nighttime heat in cities increases people's exposure to high temperatures. This can add to illness risks, especially where cooling is limited.

planet.summary: Dense buildings and paved surfaces store daytime heat and release it slowly after sunset. Limited vegetation also reduces cooling from evaporation.

economy.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.
economy.physicalLimit: Keep the previous value if changed boundaries or processing cannot be applied consistently to earlier data.

Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.

consequences: Storing or diverting river water changes when and how much water reaches places downstream. Operating rules can reduce seasonal peaks or create new daily fluctuations.
Dams can trap sediment that would otherwise reach a river delta or beach. Waves and currents may then remove coastal material faster than it is replaced.

consequences: Narrow or poorly placed stream crossings can change water speed, depth and sediment movement nearby. These are local effects that need comparison with an unobstructed stretch of stream.
Barriers at stream crossings can stop animals reaching shelter or breeding areas. Repeated isolation can reduce populations and make recovery after damage harder.

consequences: Straightening or confining rivers can move water downstream faster and separate it from floodplain storage. This changes local depths, speeds and flooding patterns.
Removing side channels and floodplain connections reduces the variety of river habitats. Fish and other wildlife may lose places to feed, breed or shelter.

Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.

planet.summary: Pumping groundwater for irrigation lowers reserves when withdrawals keep exceeding replacement. A record of water use alone does not show that an underground store is shrinking.
consequences: Irrigation pumping can reduce underground reserves when use exceeds replacement from rain, rivers or managed replenishment. Other users then have less dependable water available.
Farm pumping can intercept groundwater that would otherwise feed springs, streams or wetlands. Connected habitats may lose water during dry periods.

economy.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.

economy.physicalLimit: Missing inventories do not prove excessive pumping. Do not combine unlike underground reserves into one balance or describe dependence as an actual shortage.
economy.defaultDriver: Water pumped from underground stores to irrigate crops in a stated place and period. Pumping can reduce reserves if it exceeds replacement. This measure concerns that water use, rather than all the effects of farming.
systemLevers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

consequences: Pumping groundwater for public supplies can lower water levels if use stays above replacement. Other sources or reduced demand can change that balance. Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.

human.summary: Microbes can turn some nitrogen added to farm soil into nitrous oxide, a heat-trapping gas. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's basic method estimates 0.010 kilograms of nitrogen released in this gas per kilogram of qualifying nitrogen added, with a default uncertainty range of 0.002–0.018. Nitrous oxide traps heat and remains in the air for a long time. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates its past emissions contributed about 0.09°C of warming in 2010–2019 compared with 1850–1900, with a very likely range of about 0.05–0.16°C.
consequences: Nitrogen applied to fields but not absorbed by crops can wash away or move through soil. It may then pollute rivers, lakes or groundwater. Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
food supplies and ways of earning a living

economy.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.

economy.physicalLimit: Fertiliser produced or sold is not necessarily the amount applied to fields.

systemLevers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

human.summary: Liquid manure breaking down without oxygen produces methane. Capturing and using or destroying the gas can reduce how much escapes. Methane traps heat and has contributed to the warming already observed. The cited assessment estimates its contribution over a particular historical period, with an uncertainty range rather than one exact value.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

Ground tightly packed by cattle absorbs water less easily and may support fewer plants. Rain can then create more runoff and erosion where slopes and soil are vulnerable.
consequences: More cattle generally means more total methane from digestion within the herd. Diet and productivity change emissions per animal and per amount of food produced. Methane traps heat and has contributed to the warming already observed. The cited assessment estimates its contribution over a particular historical period, with an uncertainty range rather than one exact value.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
power, water, transport and other essential services

human.summary: Sulfur dioxide from coal burning can form fine particles downwind. Exposure to these pollutants can harm the lungs and heart, with controls affecting how much is released.
consequences: Sulfur in coal forms sulfur dioxide when the fuel burns. The amount released depends on the fuel and how effectively the plant cleans its exhaust. Some sulfur dioxide changes into tiny sulfate-containing particles in the air. These become part of fine-particle pollution.

Sulfur particles formed after coal burning reflect some sunlight and temporarily mask part of greenhouse warming. They also cause serious air pollution. Reducing them removes some cooling while improving air quality. Some airborne particles have partly offset warming by reflecting sunlight. Removing that cooling influence can add near-term warming unless the warming influence of other gases also falls enough.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

planet.summary: Sulfur in coal forms sulfur dioxide when the fuel burns. The amount released depends on the fuel and how effectively the plant cleans its exhaust.

Sulfur particles formed after coal burning reflect some sunlight and temporarily mask part of greenhouse warming. They also cause serious air pollution. Reducing them removes some cooling while improving air quality.

systemLevers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

consequences: Tightly packed soil lets less water soak in and restricts roots. More runoff can carry away topsoil where rainfall and slopes create enough force. Losing the upper layer of soil removes nutrients and reduces the ground's ability to hold water. Crops may then produce smaller or less dependable harvests.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living

human.summary: Carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity adds to the total released into the air. This record covers only the activities, places and years specified in its source, so it should not be counted again in an overlapping total. The cited assessment gives a median direct climate impact of 760 grams of CO₂-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for the assessed coal technology, with a range of 670–870. CO₂-equivalent combines gases by their warming effect. It is not a measurement of carbon dioxide alone. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
consequences: Carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity joins emissions from other sources and builds up in the atmosphere. Its contribution to warming accumulates over time, rather than staying near the place where it was released. Hotter air can make aircraft takeoff more difficult and put extra strain on runways and ground operations. The effects depend on the aircraft, airport and conditions.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services

consequences: Carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity joins emissions from other sources and builds up in the atmosphere. Its contribution to warming accumulates over time, rather than staying near the place where it was released.

systemLevers: Use energy sources that release less heat-trapping gas. Use less energy to do the same job and cut waste.
Combine standards, investment and fair financial support so workers and households can make the change.

economy.physicalLimit: A global indicator does not establish a local cause or exposure without evidence connecting it to that place.
economy.defaultDriver: The heat-trapping gas released when business and public buildings burn natural gas for heating. Building size, use and heating efficiency affect the amount. The figure applies to the buildings and period covered by the data.
systemLevers: Use energy sources that release less heat-trapping gas. Use less energy to do the same job and cut waste.
Combine standards, investment and fair financial support so workers and households can make the change.
economy.evidenceBoundary: These measures need to fit the local conditions and the people or habitats affected. The evidence does not show that every measure works everywhere.

human.summary: Carbon dioxide from burning oil to heat buildings adds to the total released into the air. This record covers only the activities, places and years specified in its source, so it should not be counted again in an overlapping total. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
consequences: Carbon dioxide from burning oil to heat buildings joins emissions from other sources and builds up in the atmosphere. Its contribution to warming accumulates over time, rather than staying near the place where it was released. Hotter air can make aircraft takeoff more difficult and put extra strain on runways and ground operations. The effects depend on the aircraft, airport and conditions.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
